name: Bali
notes: ID-BA is Bali province. Traditional walled compounds, meru shrines and clay or thatch roofs are still common in villages; the south (Denpasar, Kuta) is dense concrete and glass with grey roofs, so the palette is mixed. Rice terraces are concentrated in the central and southern uplands, not the whole island.

name: Honshu
notes: Honshu is not an ISO 3166-2 subdivision (it contains many prefectures), so no subdivisions are listed. Cherry bloom is late March to April in central Honshu; autumn colour runs roughly October to December from north to south. Snow months apply mainly to northern lowlands; Kanto and Kansai lowlands rarely hold snow. Cities are largely concrete and glass with flat grey roofs; dark tile survives in old towns.

name: Provence
notes: Provence is a cultural region, not a single ISO 3166-2 subdivision, so no code is listed. Lavender is concentrated in the Valensole and Sault plateaus and blooms late June to mid-July, not across the whole region. Hill villages and stone mas are typical, but cities and the coast are modern.

name: Norway
notes: Snow is reliable in inland and northern lowlands; the mild west coast (Bergen, Stavanger) often has little or none. Autumn birch colour is strongest in inland valleys. Modern towns are concrete and glass, though low-rise wood remains common. This is a whole-country region, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used.

name: Kenya
notes: Kenya straddles the equator; 'S' is a simplification because Nairobi and most highland farmland lie just south of it. Snow occurs only on Mt Kenya's peaks, not in the lowlands. Corrugated iron is the dominant rural roof; manyatta settlements are localized to Maasai areas. Nairobi and other cities are concrete and glass. This is a whole-country region, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used.

name: Peru, Andes highlands
notes: The Andes highlands span many valleys and elevations; terracotta tile and adobe are typical of villages, while newer towns use grey metal and concrete. Snow is on high peaks, not typical valley floors. The region crosses several departments, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is listed.

name: The Gulf
notes: The Gulf is four countries with different traditional materials (coral stone in Bahrain, mud brick and arish elsewhere). Modern cities are largely concrete and glass with beige villas, often grid-planned; wind towers survive mainly in old cores. Winter rain is irregular, so green months vary. No single ISO 3166-2 code applies. On 6 Nov: date harvest is over, palms stay green, first winter rains can start a faint green flush.

name: Netherlands
notes: Tulip fields are concentrated in the bulb districts (Bollenstreek, Noordoostpolder), not the whole country; stepped gables are mainly old canal towns. Modern districts are concrete and glass. Snow is occasional, not guaranteed every winter. This is a whole-country region, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used.

name: New England
notes: Fall colour peaks in northern New England in late September to early October and in southern coastal areas by mid-to-late October. Snow is reliable in the northern interior but less so on the southern coast. Cranberry bogs are concentrated in Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Maine, not the whole region. Boston and other cities are concrete and glass.

name: Okinawa
notes: JP-47 is Okinawa Prefecture. Traditional red clay-tile roofs, limestone walls and gusuku castles survive, but modern Okinawan homes are mostly concrete with tiled or flat roofs; Naha and the main island are densely built while the outer islands are rural. Sugarcane and pineapple are major crops, and snow does not occur.

name: Hokkaido
notes: JP-01 is Hokkaido. Snow lies from late autumn to spring and steep roofs shed it; modern farm buildings are metal-clad timber or concrete-block barns, while Ainu cise are rare today. Lavender is concentrated in the Furano and Biei area, not island-wide. Sapporo is grid-planned; most other towns are small and modern.

name: Java
notes: Java spans several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Dense kampungs with red clay-tile roofs are typical of villages and small towns, while Jakarta, Surabaya and Bandung are largely concrete and glass. Rice terraces are concentrated in the western and central highlands; tea and coffee occupy the cooler uplands. Snow does not occur.

name: Tuscany
notes: IT-52 is Tuscany. Stone farmhouses with terracotta roofs, hill towns and cypress avenues are iconic, but Florence, Siena and the coast are modern and densely built. Cypress lines are planted rather than wild forest. Snow is confined to the Apennines; autumn colour comes mainly from vines and oaks.

name: Cyclades
notes: The Cyclades are an island group, not a single ISO 3166-2 subdivision. Whitewashed cubic houses with flat roofs are typical; blue domes and doors are iconic but not universal. Santorini and Mykonos are heavily built up for tourism, while the smaller islands are sparsely settled. Snow is rare, and summer drought turns the rocky hills pale gold.

name: Rif
notes: The Rif is a cultural and geographic region, not a single ISO 3166-2 subdivision. Chefchaouen's blue medina is local, not region-wide; most houses are white or stone with red clay-tile roofs. The Rif receives Morocco's highest rainfall and is heavily forested with cedar, cork oak and fir, with terraced olives, figs and cereals. Snow lies only on the highest ridges.

name: Saharan oases and pre-Sahara
notes: The pre-Sahara and Saharan oases span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Palm groves run along the Ziz and Draa valleys, with flat-roofed earthen ksour and kasbahs; Ouarzazate and other towns are now largely concrete. Snow falls on the High Atlas but not in the oases. Dates are the signature crop; winter and early spring bring a brief green flush.

name: Oman
notes: Oman is a whole country, so no subdivision is listed. Muscat is a modern white low-rise sprawl, while interior towns and villages have mud-brick or stone courtyard houses and round-tower forts. Aflaj channels support date palms, limes and fodder. Snow is essentially absent; winter rain is irregular, and Dhofar's khareef monsoon greens the south from June to September.

name: Iran, central plateau
notes: The central plateau spans several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Yazd, Isfahan and Kashan have mud-brick cores with windcatchers and turquoise-tiled domes, but modern city edges are concrete. Qanats and bazaars support pistachios, pomegranates, wheat and dates; saffron is mainly a Khorasan crop, not a plateau-wide one. Snow is rare in low desert cities but reliable on the surrounding peaks.

name: Kerala
notes: IN-KL is Kerala. Laterite walls and steep red clay-tile roofs are typical of traditional houses, but most new buildings are concrete; the lowlands are densely settled and coconut palms dominate. Tea is confined to the high Western Ghats around Munnar, while rice, rubber and spices fill the midlands. Snow does not occur.

name: Morocco, Atlas and Middle Atlas
notes: The Atlas and Middle Atlas span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Berber villages are compact clusters of stone or rammed-earth tower houses with flat roofs; communal granaries and terraced fields are typical. Cedar forest dominates the Middle Atlas, while walnuts, almonds and cereals grow on lower terraces. Snow lies on high ground from December to March, not on valley floors; larger towns are now largely concrete.

name: Morocco, Atlantic plains and cities
notes: The Atlantic plains and cities span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Fes and Meknes retain dense medinas where green glazed-tile mosque roofs rise above white courtyard houses, while Casablanca and Rabat are predominantly white concrete, glass and Art Deco stock. The surrounding plains are Morocco's main cereal, citrus, olive and vineyard belt. Snow does not fall on the plains; summer drought turns uncultivated ground gold.

name: Saudi Arabia, Hejaz and Asir
notes: Hejaz and Asir span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Jeddah's Al-Balad has coral-stone houses with wooden roshan balconies, but most of Jeddah, Mecca and Medina is modern concrete. Asir's highlands have stone tower houses and terraced coffee, wheat and alfalfa; the Red Sea coast is hot and humid, while the mountains catch summer rain and fog. Snow is rare and confined to the highest peaks.

name: Saudi Arabia, Najd and the interior
notes: Najd and the interior span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Traditional Najdi towns have mud-brick courtyard houses with flat roofs, but Riyadh is a grid of concrete towers, villas and highways. Date oases and irrigated wheat and alfalfa are the main cultivated features, with acacia and ghaf on the sand seas and gravel plains. Winter rain is irregular; snow does not occur.

name: Iran, Caspian coast

signatureBuildings: timber house with veranda and clay-tile roof

notes: The Caspian coast spans Gilan and Mazandaran, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is Iran's wettest region, with Hyrcanian forest, rice paddies, tea gardens and citrus; villages have steep clay-tile or metal roofs and timber verandas. Rasht, Sari and other cities are now largely concrete. Snow is confined to the Alborz foothills and peaks, not the coastal plain.

name: Iran, Zagros mountains
notes: The Zagros span many provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Oak forest and steppe cover the limestone ranges, with compact stone-and-mud villages on the slopes and grain, lentil and walnut cultivation in the valleys. Snow is reliable at higher elevations from December to March. Modern towns are concrete, and nomadic pastoralism still moves between winter and summer pastures.

name: Turkey, Anatolian plateau
notes: The Anatolian plateau spans several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Dryland wheat and barley dominate the semi-arid steppe, with irrigated sugar beet and grazing in the Konya basin. Cappadocia's tuff villages include cave dwellings and flat-roofed houses; Konya and Ankara are largely modern concrete. Snow is reliable in winter, and spring brings a short green flush. Early November: gold-brown stubble with fresh winter-wheat shoots, beet harvest still running, poplars yellow.

name: Turkey, Aegean and Mediterranean coast
notes: The Aegean and Mediterranean coasts span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Bodrum's white cubic houses and Alaçatı's stone houses survive in old quarters, but Antalya, Izmir and resort strips are dominated by concrete apartment blocks and hotels. Olive groves, citrus orchards and cotton fields fill the coastal plains. Snow is essentially absent at sea level and rare on the immediate coast.

name: Egypt, Nile valley and Delta
notes: The Nile valley and Delta span many governorates, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages are dense clusters of mud-brick and concrete houses with flat roofs, often strung along canals; Cairo is a dense concrete city punctuated by minarets and domes. Irrigation supports winter wheat, berseem and beans and summer maize, rice and cotton, so the cultivated strip stays green while the surrounding desert is buff. Snow does not occur.

name: Pakistan, Punjab and Indus plains
notes: Punjab and the Indus plains span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages are compact clusters of flat-roofed brick and mud-brick houses, and Lahore's Mughal brick mosques contrast with modern concrete sprawl. Canal irrigation supports wheat, rice and cotton, with mango orchards around towns and along roads. The monsoon greens the plains from July to September; snow does not occur.

name: Yemen
notes: Yemen spans many governorates with sharply different landscapes, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Highlands are terraced and dotted with stone and mud-brick tower houses; the Tihama has date palms and flatter coastal settlements, and Hadhramaut's wadis also grow dates. Flat mud roofs dominate, with concrete increasing in towns. Qat is harvested year-round and has expanded across terraced land. Snow is rare; highland frost occurs in winter. The current conflict makes some areas inaccessible and data uncertain.

name: Jordan
notes: Jordan spans desert, highland and Jordan Valley governorates, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Amman and northern hill towns are built of pale limestone with flat concrete roofs; the Jordan Valley is irrigated and green; the eastern desert is sparse. Snow is occasional on high ground around Amman and Ajloun, not a seasonal cover. Water scarcity drives irrigation and reservoir use.

name: Israel and Palestine
notes: The region combines Israel and the Palestinian territories and crosses several districts, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is given. Mediterranean cities are dense concrete and stone-clad apartment blocks with flat roofs; red tile is a minority, mostly on older or rural buildings. The coastal plain has citrus and greenhouses, the hills olives and terraces, and the Negev is arid and sparse. Winter rain is concentrated from November to March; snow is rare and local.

name: Lebanon and Syria, coast and mountains
notes: The region covers two countries and both coastal and mountain zones, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Beirut, Damascus and Aleppo are dense concrete cities; mountain villages are stone with pitched red-tile roofs, a minority overall. Snow lies on Mount Lebanon and the coastal ranges in winter. Olives, citrus and wheat are typical, but conflict and displacement have damaged farmland and made current data uncertain.

name: Iraq, Mesopotamian plains
notes: The Tigris–Euphrates plain runs through many governorates, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages are flat-roofed mud-brick courtyards, with concrete increasingly common; turquoise-tiled domes are an iconic minority. Date palms line canals and field edges, and irrigated wheat, barley and rice occupy the plains. Summers are extremely hot and dry; winter rain is light. Salinity, upstream dams and conflict have reduced cultivation in parts. Early November: harvested stubble and freshly sown winter grain, palms green.

name: Iraq and Iran, Kurdistan highlands
notes: The Kurdistan highlands straddle northern Iraq and western Iran and cover several provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Mountain villages are stone or mud-brick with flat roofs, increasingly covered with pitched corrugated metal; Erbil, Sulaymaniyah and Sanandaj have sprawling concrete outskirts. Oak woodland, orchards and cereals fill the valleys, and snow covers high ground in winter. Cross-border statistics are uneven.

name: Afghanistan
notes: Afghanistan covers very diverse terrain, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Rural settlements are walled mud-brick compounds with flat roofs, often with a corner tower; blue-tiled domes are an iconic minority. Kabul and other cities are mostly low concrete blocks with some glass buildings. Irrigated valleys grow wheat, barley, fruit and grapes, while the Hindu Kush and central highlands carry snow for months. Drought, conflict and displacement make conditions variable and current figures uncertain.

name: Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan lowlands
notes: This region combines the Kara Kum, the Amu Darya oases and the Zarafshan–Fergana lowlands across three countries, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Towns and villages are low adobe courtyard houses with flat roofs, while Tashkent and provincial capitals are dominated by Soviet-era concrete blocks; turquoise-tiled madrasa domes are an iconic minority in Samarkand and Bukhara. Irrigation supports cotton, wheat, melons and orchards. Winters are cold enough for snow on the lowlands; summers are hot and dry, and the Aral Sea shrinkage has left salt and dust problems.

name: Caucasus, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan
notes: The Caucasus region spans Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan and several provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Tbilisi, Yerevan and Baku are largely concrete cities; villages mix flat concrete roofs with pitched red tile or metal. Stone churches with conical domes and timber-balcony houses are typical. The Black Sea coast is humid and green, the Kura–Araxes basin dry, and high ground holds snow from December to March. Vineyards and orchards are widespread.

name: India, Rajasthan and the Thar Desert
notes: Rajasthan and the Thar span the whole state and adjoining desert districts, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Towns are built of flat-roofed sandstone or concrete courtyard houses; havelis with jharokha balconies are an urban signature. The Thar is sand dunes and thorn scrub, greening briefly with the July–September monsoon. Wheat and mustard are winter crops, bajra is sown with the monsoon, and cotton follows the rains. Jaipur and other cities are now largely concrete and glass.

name: India, Indo-Gangetic plain

signatureBuildings: north Indian temple with shikhara tower

notes: The Indo-Gangetic plain covers Delhi, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages are compact brick-and-plaster courtyard houses with flat roofs; Delhi and the larger cities are dense concrete and glass. Wheat, rice and sugarcane dominate the alluvial fields, with mango, banyan and neem trees. The monsoon runs from June to September and brings floods to the eastern plain; summers are very hot and winters cool. Groundwater depletion and air pollution are growing problems.

name: India, Deccan plateau
notes: The Deccan plateau spans Maharashtra, Telangana and interior Karnataka, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Basalt stone and mud-brick courtyard houses with flat roofs are typical of villages, while Pune, Hyderabad and Bengaluru are largely concrete and glass. Cotton, sorghum and irrigated sugarcane grow on the black and red soils. The monsoon arrives from June to September; March to May is hot and dry. Hill forts and temple towns are characteristic, and water storage is a persistent concern.

name: India, Tamil Nadu and the southeast coast
notes: Tamil Nadu and the southeast coast form a hot, humid region with both southwest and northeast monsoons, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages have whitewashed walls and pitched terracotta-tile roofs; Chennai and other cities are dense concrete and glass. Rice, sugarcane and groundnut are the main crops, with coconut palms along the coast. The northeast monsoon brings the heaviest rain and cyclones from October to December. Temple gateway towers are a regional signature.

name: India, Himalaya and Kashmir (including Ladakh)
notes: The Indian Himalaya here includes Kashmir and Ladakh, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Kashmir's valley has irrigated rice, apples and saffron and houses of stone, mud and timber with pitched metal roofs; Ladakh is a high cold desert of barley, apricot and willow with flat mud roofs. Srinagar and Leh have sprawling concrete outskirts. Snow lies on high ground for months, and winter closes many passes. The political status of Kashmir remains disputed, so data is uneven.

name: India, Northeast and Bengal
notes: This region covers West Bengal and Assam, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Rural houses are bamboo or wood on raised plinths with pitched corrugated-metal roofs; Kolkata and Guwahati are dense concrete cities. Rice, jute and tea are the main crops, and tea gardens cover the Assam and Darjeeling hills. The monsoon is long and heavy, causing floods and landslides. Thatch survives as a minority roof material, and the Sundarbans mangroves fringe the coast.

name: Pakistan, Sindh and Balochistan
notes: Sindh and Balochistan differ sharply: Sindh is an irrigated Indus plain, while Balochistan is a dry, sparsely populated plateau, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages are mud-brick courtyard houses with flat roofs, with concrete and rusted metal increasing in towns; Karachi is a dense concrete and glass metropolis. Cotton, rice and wheat grow under canal irrigation, and date palms line fields and channels. Sindh's monsoon is weak, while Balochistan gets winter rain and snow on high ground. Water scarcity and salinity are severe.

name: Pakistan, northern mountains
notes: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan form Pakistan's northern mountain belt, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Villages are stone or mud-brick houses with flat roofs and timber balconies, often terraced into steep slopes, with rusted metal roofs increasing in towns; Peshawar is a dense brick-and-concrete city. Wheat, maize and apricot, apple and walnut orchards fill the valleys. Snow covers high ground from November to March, and many passes close in winter. Remote terrain makes data sparse and uneven.

name: Nepal and Bhutan
notes: Nepal and Bhutan span the Terai plains, terraced middle hills and high Himalaya, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Traditional houses are rammed earth or stone with pitched corrugated-metal or slate roofs; Kathmandu has dense concrete sprawl, while Thimphu remains a compact town of traditional facades. Rice, maize and wheat are the staple crops, with terraces and irrigation channels on the hillsides. The monsoon runs from June to September; snow lies high up in winter. Bhutan's dzongs and Nepal's pagoda temples are regional signatures.

name: Bangladesh
notes: Bangladesh is a densely populated delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Rural houses are bamboo or wood on raised plinths with pitched corrugated-metal roofs; Dhaka is a dense concrete and glass city. Rice and jute dominate agriculture, with tea in the Sylhet hills, and much of the land is flooded in the monsoon. Cyclones and river erosion are recurring hazards. Thatch survives as a minority roofing material, and the Sundarbans mangroves fringe the southwest coast.

name: Sri Lanka and the Maldives

signatureBuildings: whitewashed house with clay tile roof

notes: Sri Lanka and the Maldives are Indian Ocean island states, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Sri Lanka's wet zone has whitewashed houses with clay-tile roofs, tea estates and rice paddies; the dry zone is drier and more sparsely settled. The Maldives is a chain of low coral atolls with dense concrete and metal roofs, coconut palms and limited taro, banana and fruit cultivation. Colombo and Malé are dense urban centres. Monsoons bring rain at different times, and sea-level rise threatens the Maldives.

name: China, North China Plain
notes: The North China Plain covers Beijing, Hebei, Shandong and Henan, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. It is one of the most densely populated rural regions on Earth: villages are compact brick courtyard houses, mostly with flat concrete roofs used for drying grain, while older grey-tile roofs survive in Beijing's hutongs and market towns. Beijing and Tianjin are dense concrete-and-glass cities. Winter wheat, summer maize and cotton dominate the fields, with poplar shelterbelts and jujube trees. Winters are cold and dry with light snow; summers are hot and humid under the East Asian monsoon. Groundwater depletion, subsidence and air pollution are serious.

name: China, Yangtze delta and lower Yangtze

signatureBuildings: whitewashed canal-side house with dark tile roof
shikumen lane house with stone gate

notes: This entry covers Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The delta is one of China's most urbanised regions: Shanghai and the Suzhou-Wuxi-Changzhou corridor are dense concrete and glass, while canal water towns retain whitewashed walls and dark tile roofs. Rice, rapeseed, tea and mulberry are the traditional crops, and camphor, willow and bamboo line the waterways. The climate is humid subtropical with plum rains in June and July and typhoons in late summer. Land subsidence, flooding and pollution are growing problems.

name: China, south (Guangdong, Guangxi and Fujian)
notes: Guangdong, Guangxi and Fujian are grouped here, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The Pearl River Delta is a near-continuous urban belt of concrete and glass, but karst valleys in Guangxi have stilted timber houses, Fujian has rammed-earth tulou rings, and Lingnan towns keep narrow, shaded shophouses with dark tile roofs. Double-cropped rice, sugarcane and lychee and citrus orchards fill the lowlands, with banyan and bamboo throughout. The subtropical monsoon brings heavy rain from April to September and typhoons in late summer; lowland frost and snow are essentially absent. Quarrying and rapid urban sprawl are pressures.

name: China, Sichuan basin and Yunnan

signatureBuildings: whitewashed timber house with thin tiled roof

notes: The Sichuan basin and Yunnan are combined here, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The basin is humid, cloudy and densely farmed, with thin light tiled roofs and whitewashed timber frames; Chengdu and Chongqing are dense concrete cities. Yunnan is a mild plateau of terraced rice, tobacco and tea, with stone and timber houses and flat mud roofs in its Tibetan borderlands. Snow falls only on high ground. The region is seismically active, and ethnic diversity makes local building styles highly variable.

name: China, Tibetan plateau

signatureBuildings: whitewashed stone house with flat roof
monastery with white walls and flat roofs

notes: The Tibetan plateau entry covers the Tibet Autonomous Region and adjacent highlands, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Settlements are sparse, clustered on south-facing slopes, with whitewashed stone or mud-brick houses and flat roofs in the dry central and western plateau; eastern valleys use pitched slate or tile. Monasteries with white walls, dark window bands and prayer flags are the signature structures. Highland barley, wheat and rapeseed grow in irrigated valley fields, and yaks graze the steppe. Snow, thin air and a short growing season limit everything; road and rail access has improved but data remains uneven.

name: China, Xinjiang and Gansu (deserts and oases)
notes: Xinjiang and Gansu form a vast arid belt of deserts, basins and oasis chains, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Oasis villages are compact mud-brick courtyard houses with flat roofs, and mosques with domes and minarets mark the towns; Ürümqi and Lanzhou are dense high-rise cities. Cotton, wheat, grapes and melons grow under irrigation, with poplar shelterbelts along canals. Winters are cold and summers very hot and dry, with sandstorms in spring. Water scarcity and the sensitive political situation make reliable local data hard to obtain.

name: China, northeast (Manchuria) and Inner Mongolia

signatureBuildings: brick house with pitched metal roof

notes: Northeast China and Inner Mongolia are combined here, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Manchuria is a grain belt of maize, soybean and rice on black soil, with brick houses with pitched metal or tile roofs and kang heating; Harbin, Changchun and Shenyang are dense high-rise cities. Inner Mongolia's steppe is sparsely settled with felt gers and livestock, though coal and rare-earth towns have grown quickly. Winters are long and severely cold, summers short and warm; snow lies from November to March. Desertification and dust storms affect the western steppe.

name: Mongolia
notes: Mongolia is a landlocked country of steppe, forest and Gobi desert. No ISO 3166-2 subdivisions are listed because this entry covers the whole country. Most herders live in felt gers, while Ulaanbaatar is dominated by Soviet-era apartment blocks and new high-rise towers. Wheat, barley and potatoes grow in the northern river valleys, and livestock grazing is the main land use. Winters are extremely cold and dry, summers short and warm; dzud winters can kill large numbers of animals. Mining, air pollution in Ulaanbaatar and desertification are major pressures.

name: Korea (South and North)
notes: This entry covers both South and North Korea. No ISO 3166-2 subdivisions are listed because the entry groups the two countries. Traditional hanok houses have dark clay-tile roofs, white plaster walls and ondol underfloor heating. South Korea is dominated by dense high-rise apartment cities, while North Korea remains more rural, with high-rise blocks concentrated in Pyongyang. Rice, maize, vegetables and ginseng are grown in the South; the North relies more on maize, potatoes and rice. The monsoon brings jangma rains in June and July and typhoons in late summer, while winters are cold and dry with snow. The militarised border and limited data from North Korea make regional averages uncertain.

name: Taiwan

signatureBuildings: red-brick house with clay tile roof

notes: Taiwan is a densely populated subtropical island. No ISO 3166-2 subdivisions are listed because the entry covers the whole island, whose political status is disputed. The western lowlands are a near-continuous concrete city, with red-brick houses and clay-tile roofs surviving in older towns and aboriginal stone or thatch structures in the mountains. Rice, tea, sugarcane and fruit are the main crops. Typhoons and earthquakes are recurring hazards, and the central mountains rise above 3,000 m and get winter snow. Data is good for the lowlands but uneven for remote mountain districts.

name: Japan, Kyushu and Shikoku

signatureBuildings: timber house with dark kawara tile roof

notes: Kyushu and Shikoku span several prefectures, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Both islands are densely settled in the lowlands, with Fukuoka, Kitakyushu, Matsuyama and Takamatsu forming dense concrete and glass cities; older towns retain timber machiya and farmhouses with deep eaves and dark kawara tiles. Rice, tea and citrus are the main crops, with terraced fields on the hillsides and mandarins on the warmer coasts. The climate is humid subtropical with a June-July rainy season and late-summer typhoons; snow is not typical in the lowlands and falls mainly on the mountains. Depopulation, coastal erosion and typhoon damage are growing concerns.

name: Vietnam, north (Red River delta, karst and terraces)

signatureBuildings: brick courtyard house with clay tile roof
stilted timber house on karst slope

notes: The Red River delta, northern karst and terraced highlands span several provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Delta villages are compact brick and plaster courtyard houses with red clay tile roofs, while Hanoi and Haiphong are dense concrete and glass cities; karst valleys use stilted timber houses and stone terraces. Rice, maize and tea are the main crops, with vegetables and fruit in the delta. The north has a humid subtropical monsoon climate with a cool, damp winter and a hot, wet summer; snow is not typical in the lowlands. Dike failure, flooding and urban pollution are persistent risks.

name: Vietnam, centre and south (Mekong delta)

signatureBuildings: stilt house with corrugated metal roof
garden house with clay tile roof

notes: Central Vietnam and the Mekong delta span many provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The delta is a dense network of canals, stilt houses and rice fields, with corrugated metal and clay tile roofs; Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang are dense concrete and glass. Rice, coconut and sugarcane dominate the lowlands, with coffee and pepper in the central highlands. The south has a tropical monsoon climate with a May-October wet season and a December-April dry season, while the central coast is prone to typhoons and floods. Saltwater intrusion and land subsidence are serious in the delta.

name: Thailand

signatureBuildings: stilted timber house with pitched tile roof

notes: Thailand is covered as a whole; no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used because the entry covers the country. Villages in the central plain and north are clusters of stilted timber houses with pitched tile or metal roofs, while Bangkok and the industrial estates are dense concrete and glass. Rice, sugarcane and rubber are the main crops, with orchards and cassava on the uplands. The climate is tropical monsoon with a May-October wet season and a November-April dry season; the south is wetter and typhoons are rare. Flooding, coastal erosion and air pollution are recurring problems.

name: Laos and Cambodia

signatureBuildings: stilted timber house with pitched roof

notes: Laos and Cambodia are grouped here, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Both are predominantly rural: stilted timber and bamboo houses with pitched metal or thatch roofs line the Mekong and its tributaries, while Vientiane and Phnom Penh are low-rise concrete cities with a few new high-rises. Rice, cassava and maize are the main crops, with fishing and river gardens along the floodplains. The climate is tropical monsoon with a May-October wet season and a November-April dry season; snow never occurs. Dam building, deforestation and Mekong flow changes are major pressures.

name: Myanmar

signatureBuildings: stilted bamboo house with thatched roof

notes: Myanmar is covered as a whole; no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used because the entry covers the country. Villages are mostly stilted bamboo or timber houses with thatch or corrugated metal roofs, and monasteries with tiered roofs mark the towns; Yangon and Mandalay are dense concrete and brick cities. Rice, pulses and sesame are the main crops, with a dry zone in the centre and monsoon forest along the coasts. The climate is tropical monsoon with a May-October wet season and a November-April dry season; snow is confined to the northern highlands and is not typical in the lowlands. Conflict, displacement and deforestation make data uneven.

name: Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore

signatureBuildings: Malay stilt house with pitched roof

notes: Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore are grouped here, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Kampung houses are raised on stilts with pitched roofs, Chinese shophouses line the old town centres, and Singapore and Kuala Lumpur are dense high-rise concrete and glass cities. Oil palm, rice and rubber are the main crops, with coconut and fruit along the coasts. The climate is equatorial with rain throughout the year and no marked dry season; snow never occurs. Deforestation, peat fires and sea-level rise are regional concerns.

name: Borneo (Sarawak, Sabah, Kalimantan and Brunei)
notes: Borneo spans Sarawak, Sabah, Kalimantan and Brunei, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The island straddles the equator; S is a simplification because most of Kalimantan lies south of it while Sarawak, Sabah and Brunei lie north. Interior Dayak longhouses are stilted timber buildings with pitched metal or thatch roofs, coastal Malay villages use similar stilt houses, and Kuching, Kota Kinabalu, Balikpapan and Bandar Seri Begawan are dense concrete cities. Oil palm, rice and pepper are the main crops, with logging and plantations replacing rainforest. The climate is equatorial with heavy rain throughout the year and no marked dry season; snow never occurs. Deforestation, peat fires and habitat loss are severe.

name: Indonesia, Sumatra

signatureBuildings: Batak house with steep saddleback roof
Minangkabau house with curved horn roof

notes: Sumatra spans several Indonesian provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The island straddles the equator; N is a simplification because most of the population lives north of it. Villages along the rivers and roads mix stilted Malay houses with the steep saddleback roofs of Batak houses and the curved horn roofs of Minangkabau houses; Medan and Palembang are dense concrete cities. Oil palm, rice and coffee are the main crops, with rubber and mangrove forests. The west coast is wet year-round, while the east coast has a drier mid-year season; snow never occurs. Deforestation and peat fires cause recurrent haze.

name: Philippines

signatureBuildings: stilted bamboo house with thatched roof
stone-and-timber colonial house with tile roof

notes: The Philippines is an archipelago of many provinces, so no single ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Lowland villages mix stilted bamboo bahay kubo with concrete and metal houses, older towns retain stone-and-timber colonial houses with tile roofs, and Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao are dense concrete and glass cities. Rice, coconut and sugarcane are the main crops, with banana, pineapple and mango for export. The climate is tropical maritime with a May-October southwest monsoon and a November-April dry season; typhoons are frequent in the north and snow never occurs. Deforestation, coastal erosion and typhoon damage are major risks.

name: Southern England

signatureCrops.name: pasture and small fields divided by hedgerows (bocage)

notes: Most widespread modern look is grey-brown concrete tile and brick on post-war estates, plus grey flat-roof sprawl around London and the motorway corridors; red clay tile, slate and flint dominate older villages and thatch survives as an iconic minority. The chalk downs (South Downs/North Downs) show open, larger stripier fields; the Weald and west keep small hedged patchwork. Landscape stays green all year with no dry season. England is split by latitude (about 53°N) from the northern region; no ISO code separates them.

name: Northern England, Wales and Scotland

signatureCrops.name: sheep pasture and heather moorland with dry-stone walls

notes: Reads as dark blue-green moorland and small drystone-walled pasture cells; block plantations of Sitka spruce appear as uniform dark rectangles. Heather moors bloom purple August-September and bracken turns orange-brown on the hills in autumn. Lowland snow is typical in Scotland and the Pennines, less reliable in Wales. Stone terraces and mills mark the former industrial valleys; the Highlands are among Europe's most sparsely populated areas. Northern England (north of about 53°N) also belongs here.

name: Ireland

signatureCrops.name: permanent grassland for cattle and sheep in hedgerow fields

notes: The whole island reads as one continuous green quilt of small hedged fields (bocage); trees are mostly hedgerow trees and dark spruce plantation blocks. Blanket bog and cutaway peat show as brown patches, especially in the west and midlands. One-off whitewashed or cream-rendered houses string along roads outside villages. Grey slate roofs dominate, red tile an urban minority; lowland snow is uncommon and autumn colour is weak.

name: Northern France (Normandy, Brittany, Paris basin)

signatureCrops.name: openfield cereals and oilseed rape (Paris basin, Beauce)

notes: Two landscapes: bocage hedgerow country with half-timbered and stone farmhouses in Normandy and Brittany, and the almost treeless, huge open fields of the Paris basin and Beauce, one of France's most productive grain areas. Slate roofs prevail in the west, terracotta in the Ile-de-France; thatch is an iconic Normandy minority. Apple orchards show pink-white blossom in April.

name: South-west France and the Massif Central
notes: Terracotta roofs and ochre limestone dominate; the Auvergne part of the Massif Central adds dark volcanic stone, grey lauze roofs and extinct-volcano silhouettes. Bastide towns are regular grids with arcaded squares; the rest is scattered hamlets. The Landes maritime-pine forest is one solid dark-green block south-west of Bordeaux. Vineyards redden the slopes in October.

name: Central Spain (Castile, Madrid, La Mancha)

signatureCrops.name: dry cereals with fallow strips (wheat, barley)

notes: Huge, empty high plains ringed by mountains, very sparsely populated; from late June to October everything reads yellow-ochre, with only a brief spring green. Villages are compact grids built around a stone church tower. Madrid and provincial cities add grey flat-roofed concrete blocks. Autumn colour is limited to gold poplars along rivers in late October; lowland snow falls most winters.

name: Andalusia and the Mediterranean coast
notes: Pueblos blancos sit dense on hilltops, defined by whitewashed walls and red-brown tiled roofs; the coast is low-rise resort sprawl with grey flat roofs, and the Poniente Almeriense is a sheet of white plastic greenhouses visible from orbit. Olive groves are the region's main canopy, pale grey-green. Sierra Nevada holds snow into June but lowland snow is rare; hills turn gold from June to October with a brief green spring.

name: Portugal

signatureCrops.name: montado: cork oak savanna with grazing

notes: Terracotta roofs over whitewash from the air; Lisbon adds red-roofed hills. The north is greener with granite walls, scattered hamlets and schist villages; the Alentejo is a golden plain studded with widely spaced cork oaks (montado). The Alto Douro wine region shows its stepped vineyards as a World Heritage landscape. Autumn colour is limited to vineyards and some chestnut country; lowland snow is rare.

name: Northern Italy (Po valley, Lombardy, Veneto, Italian Alps)
notes: Europe's largest fully cultivated plain: nearly every roof is terracotta, interrupted only by grey modern blocks around Milan and other cities. Dense grid towns with a campanile, scattered cascina farmsteads, poplar rows and flooded rice mirrors around Vercelli-Novara in spring. Winter haze and fog sit over the valley; the Alpine flank above is dark conifer and grey rock. The Conegliano-Valdobbiadene hills are a UNESCO vineyard landscape.

name: Southern Italy and Sicily
notes: Hilltop towns of cream and ochre stucco with terracotta roofs; whitewashed trulli with grey stone cones around Alberobello in Apulia; black lava fields on Etna's flanks. Pale grey-green olive canopies are the most common tree cover; the interior turns gold from June to October and greens again with winter rains. Almond groves flower pink in February; modern outskirt blocks are concrete with grey flat roofs.

name: Indonesia, Sulawesi and Maluku

signatureBuildings: stilted timber house with thatched roof

notes: Sulawesi and Maluku span several Indonesian provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Sulawesi's four peninsulas and Maluku's scattered islands mix stilted timber houses, dark saddleback roofs and thatched village houses; Makassar, Manado and Ambon are dense concrete cities. The region straddles the equator, so S is a simplification. Roofing is mixed: corrugated metal dominates towns and coastal roads, while dark thatch survives on traditional houses. Rice, coconut and cloves are the main visible crops, with sago, nutmeg, coffee and cocoa in the hills. The climate is equatorial with rain in most months and only a weak dry season; snow never occurs. Data for Maluku's outer islands is thin, and logging, mining and sea-level rise are growing pressures.

name: Indonesia, Nusa Tenggara and Timor-Leste

signatureBuildings: stilted timber house with steep thatched roof
timber house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Nusa Tenggara and Timor-Leste span many islands and provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The region is mostly dry monsoon country: stilted timber houses with steep thatch roofs in Sumba and Lombok, corrugated metal and clay tile in towns, and dense low-rise concrete in Mataram, Kupang and Dili. Roofing is mixed: thatch dominates rural villages, while corrugated metal and clay tile are common in towns. Rice, maize and coffee are the main crops, with cassava, coconut and sandalwood on drier slopes. The wet season runs from December to April and the dry season from May to November; snow never occurs. Water scarcity, deforestation and poor roads make data uneven.

name: New Guinea (Papua and Papua New Guinea)

signatureBuildings: stilted timber house with thatched roof

notes: New Guinea is split between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The island is dominated by the highlands and by lowland rainforest, with stilted timber and thatched houses in villages and corrugated metal in towns; Port Moresby and Jayapura are the largest cities. The island straddles the equator, so S is a simplification. Roofing is mostly thatch in villages, with corrugated metal in towns and along roads. Sweet potato, taro and coffee are the main crops, with sago, banana and coconut in the lowlands. The climate is warm and humid year-round with only weak seasonal variation; snow occurs only on the highest peaks and is not typical in the lowlands. Road access, conflict and deforestation make data uneven.

name: Australia, east coast (Queensland to Victoria)

signatureBuildings: timber house on stumps with corrugated iron roof
brick bungalow with terracotta tile roof

notes: The east coast from Queensland to Victoria spans several states, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The coast is Australia's most densely settled strip: timber Queenslanders on stumps, brick bungalows with terracotta tiles, and dense concrete and glass in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. Roofs are mostly corrugated metal, with terracotta tile in older suburbs and charcoal painted metal in newer ones. Sugarcane, wheat and grapes are the main crops, with dairy, cotton and horticulture in the hinterland. The climate ranges from subtropical in Queensland to temperate in Victoria, with wet summers in the north and winter rain in the south; snow is not typical in the lowlands. Coastal erosion, bushfires and housing pressure are recurring issues.

name: Australia, interior and outback

signatureBuildings: corrugated iron house with wide verandah

notes: The interior and outback span several states and territories, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is a sparsely populated region of red plains, ranges and saltbush, with corrugated iron houses, wide verandahs and small mining or pastoral towns; Alice Springs is the main inland centre. Roofs are mostly corrugated metal, often weathered silver or rust red. Wheat, sorghum and cotton grow on the margins, while cattle and sheep graze the vast stations. The north has a summer monsoon, the centre is arid and the south gets winter rain; snow is not typical in the lowlands. Heat, drought, dust and very long distances shape daily life.

name: Australia, south-west and Tasmania

signatureBuildings: timber cottage with corrugated iron roof

notes: South-west Australia and Tasmania are grouped here, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The south-west has Mediterranean jarrah and karri forest, wheat and wine, while Tasmania has cool temperate rainforest, dairy, orchards and hydro towns; Perth, Hobart and Launceston are the main cities. Roofs are mostly corrugated metal, with terracotta and slate as older minority types. The south-west has wet winters and dry summers, Tasmania has rain in most months and cool summers; lowland snow is not typical. Bushfires, dieback and water stress are persistent concerns.

name: New Zealand, North Island

signatureBuildings: timber villa with corrugated iron roof

notes: The North Island spans several regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. It is the more populous island, with Auckland, Wellington and Hamilton forming dense low-rise cities, and rural towns built largely of timber weatherboard with corrugated iron roofs. Roofs are mostly dark painted metal or corrugated iron, with terracotta tile on older villas. Dairy pasture, kiwifruit and maize are the main crops, with pine forestry and sheep on the hills. The climate is temperate maritime with rain in most months and mild winters; snow is not typical in the lowlands. Volcanic risk, earthquakes and housing pressure are significant.

name: New Zealand, South Island

signatureBuildings: stone cottage with dark iron roof

notes: The South Island spans several regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The Southern Alps divide the island into wet rainforest in the west and drier Canterbury Plains and Central Otago in the east; Christchurch, Dunedin and Nelson are the main cities. Timber villas with iron roofs, stone cottages and modern low-rise housing sit among dairy pasture, wheat, vineyards and orchards. Roofs are mostly corrugated metal, with slate and terracotta on older buildings. The climate is oceanic, with rain throughout the year in the west and drier summers in the east; snow is common on the mountains but not typical in the lowlands. Earthquake risk, irrigation pressure and tourism are major issues.

name: Pacific islands, Melanesia and Polynesia (Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and French Polynesia)

signatureBuildings: stilted timber house with thatched roof
concrete block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and French Polynesia are grouped here, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The islands are mostly coastal villages of timber and concrete block, plus traditional thatched meeting houses and open-sided fales; Suva, Apia, Nuku'alofa and Papeete are the main towns. Corrugated metal is now the majority roof, with thatch surviving on traditional houses. Coconut, taro and sugarcane are the main crops, with vanilla, breadfruit and fishing. The climate is tropical maritime with a November-April wet season, a May-October dry season and frequent cyclones; snow never occurs. The group spans Melanesia and Polynesia, so data is uneven and sea-level rise is a serious threat.

name: Hawaii

signatureBuildings: single-wall timber plantation house with corrugated iron roof

notes: Hawaii is a U.S. state spanning the Hawaiian Islands, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Honolulu is a dense high-rise city, while the outer islands remain low-rise with single-wall timber plantation houses, stucco and concrete block. Corrugated metal is the common roof, with asphalt shingle and clay tile in older and newer suburbs. Coffee, pineapple and macadamia are the main crops, with taro, cattle and horticulture. The climate is tropical with trade winds, a wet October-April season and a drier May-September season; snow falls on the highest peaks but is not typical in the lowlands. Volcanic risk, invasive species and water supply are key concerns.

name: Northern Germany (North German Plain)

signatureCrops.name: cereals, sugar beet and oilseed rape, large open fields

notes: Glacial plain: huge loess-borde arable blocks east of the Elbe, sandy pine-birch geest and heath (Lüneburg Heath blooms yellow-purple August-September), the Mecklenburg lakeland, and dike-lined marsh strips whose villages run as single street rows (Marschhufendorf). Red brick dominates walls and Gothic church spires; thatch survives on Frisian farmhouses. Hamburg and Berlin add grey flat-roofed modern sprawl, and wind turbines are everywhere. Lowland snow occurs most winters but is increasingly brief. North Rhine-Westphalia, Bremen and Saxony-Anhalt were added here by Claude (the Ruhr is dense brick and concrete).

name: Southern Germany (Bavaria, Black Forest, Rhine valley)

signatureCrops.name: meadows and maize on the alpine foreland

notes: The classic southern German look from the air: light plaster walls under steep red tile roofs in nucleated church villages, very steep roofs on old Black Forest farms (some wood-shingled), dark spruce forest covering the Mittelgebirge, deep green meadows, hop gardens in the Hallertau and terraced Rhine vineyards. Munich and Stuttgart bring grey flat-roofed modern districts. Lowland snow is normal in winter. Hesse, Thuringia and Saxony were added here by Claude (forested uplands, red-roofed villages).

name: Belgium and Luxembourg

signatureCrops.name: small hedged arable and pasture fields

notes: Covers all of Belgium and Luxembourg. Flanders is one of Europe's densest rural mosaics: small brick farmsteads with red roofs strung in ribbons along every road and canal, poplar rows and pollarded willows. The Ardennes (Belgian southeast, Luxembourg's Eislek) turn to forested hills with stone houses and slate; the Moselle shows terraced vines. Modern zones are grey flat roofs. Lowland snow is occasional and brief, more regular on the Ardennes plateau.

name: Switzerland and Austria (Alps)

signatureCrops.name: orchards and small fields on valley floors

notes: Covers all of Switzerland, Austria and Liechtenstein. From the air: grey rock and snowfields above dark spruce forest, bright fresh-green hay meadows in a mosaic up the slopes, scattered white plaster and dark timber chalets in hamlets, steep dark roofs. Larch forest turns gold in October, the region's clearest autumn show. Wide valley floors carry nucleated villages, orchards (Mostviertel, Rheintal) and modern grey-roofed towns (Zurich, Vienna basin). East of the Alps the land flattens into large grain fields with wind turbines (Weinviertel).

name: Denmark
notes: Almost treeless rolling plain, flat and open, with medium-large fields in bright greens and blocks of rape-yellow; hedgerows are few. Red brick farmhouses and red tile roofs; whitewashed village churches with green copper spires, thatch surviving in the southwest. Conifer plantations and summerhouse clusters (grey roofs) along the west coast; offshore wind farms on the horizon. Climate is mild maritime: winter snow falls occasionally but does not linger.

name: Southern Sweden (Skåne to Stockholm)

signatureCrops.name: cereals, rape and sugar beet, large open fields (Skåne plain)

notes: Two halves: the Skåne plain, with big yellow-green and rape-yellow fields, poplar and oak avenues and few woods, and the forested lake-and-boulder country of Småland. Falu-red wooden farmhouses with dark roofs are the signature; village churches are whitewashed with dark spires. Öland and Gotland show pale limestone alvar plains. Stockholm and Malmö are grey modern sprawl with dark flat roofs. Autumn comes early: gold birches in late September-October; snow falls most winters but often melts.

name: Northern Sweden and Finland
notes: Swedish counties for the northern half only; covers all of Finland. From the air this is one dark blue-green boreal forest stitched with thousands of smooth lakes (Finnish Lakeland: drumlins and eskers between long sinuous waters) and pale square clearcut patches. Settlement is scattered red-timber farms with grey metal roofs; towns are grey concrete and modern. Birch turns gold in September. Lowland snow cover typically lasts November to March. The Åland Islands (AX), Finnish and Swedish-speaking, share this look: red timber houses on granite skerries.

name: Iceland
notes: signatureTrees is empty on purpose: the island is essentially treeless (deforestation since settlement; native birch survives only in scrub and rare plantations). The air view is volcanic: black lava fields furred with grey-green moss, pale glacial outwash plains, braided glacial rivers, icefields. Isolated white and brightly painted corrugated-metal farmhouses with bright green fertilised hay strips; turf-roofed houses survive as heritage. Reykjavík is a modern concrete and metal city.

name: Poland
notes: The air signature is fragmentation: countless narrow strip fields forming a grey-green-brown quilt (finest in the former Austrian and Russian partitions), against large uniform blocks in the west. Red tile roofs over cream-rendered and brick houses in chain villages along roads; dark pine plantations and birch on sandy soils; the Masurian lakeland in the northeast; the Sudetes and Carpathians in the south. Cities add grey flat-roofed panel-block and glass districts. Lowland snow falls most winters.

name: Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary
notes: Covers all three countries. Czechia's defining air view is the sea of small red tile roofs around cream-rendered village churches, on wooded Bohemian-Moravian hills; Slovakia adds chain villages climbing into the Carpathians with spruce forest and scattered hamlets. The Hungarian Great Plain (puszta: treeless steppe with grey cattle and tanya farmsteads around Hortobágy) shows huge uniform dry fields that go straw-gold in July-August, with locust groves flowering white in May and poplar windbreaks. Prague, Bratislava and Budapest bring grey modern sprawl.

name: Algeria and Tunisia, coast and Tell Atlas

signatureBuildings: stone house with terracotta tile roof

notes: Algeria and Tunisia span many provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The Tell Atlas runs parallel to the Mediterranean coast, with whitewashed flat-roof houses and courtyard medinas in Algiers, Tunis and the hill towns, and terracotta tile roofs in Kabyle villages and French colonial quarters. Olive groves, wheat and grapes are the main visible crops, with citrus and dates on the warmer coast. Winters are mild and wet and summers hot and dry; snow falls on the high Atlas but is not typical in the lowlands. Water stress, wildfire and coastal development are growing pressures. Algeria south of about 34°N belongs to the Sahara region (split by latitude).

name: Sahara (Algeria, Libya, Niger, Mali and Mauritania)
notes: The Sahara spans five countries, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is hyper-arid rock, gravel and dune country with scattered oases where flat-roofed mud-brick houses, courtyard compounds and palm-thatch shelters cluster around wells and date gardens. Date palms, acacia and tamarisk are the main trees; barley, dates and small irrigated vegetable plots are the visible crops. Rain is rare and irregular, summer heat is extreme and winter nights are cold; snow does not occur in the lowlands. Nomadic herding, oil and gas, and remote borders shape the region, and population data is sparse. Shares countries with the Tell (north of about 34°N), the Libyan coast (north of about 31°N) and the Sahel (south of about 16°N); split by latitude.

name: Libya, coast

signatureBuildings: Italian colonial villa with tile roof

notes: Libya's coast spans several districts, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The narrow Mediterranean strip around Tripoli, Misrata and Benghazi has whitewashed flat-roof houses, courtyard medinas and Italian colonial villas with terracotta tiles, backed by olive groves and date palms. Barley, olives and dates are the main crops, with figs and vegetables in gardens. Winters are mild and wet and summers hot and dry; the desert hinterland is rainless and snow is not typical in the lowlands. Conflict, water scarcity and coastal erosion make data uneven. Libya south of about 31°N belongs to the Sahara region (split by latitude).

name: Sudan and South Sudan
notes: Sudan and South Sudan span many states, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The north is desert and semi-desert Nile country with flat-roofed mud-brick houses and courtyard compounds; the south is savanna and floodplain with round thatched tukuls and scattered farms. Sorghum, millet and cotton are the main crops, with gum arabic, sesame and date palms; Khartoum and Juba are the largest cities. Rain comes from June to September in the north and May to October in the south, and snow never occurs in the lowlands. Conflict, displacement and uncertain rainfall make data uneven.

name: Ethiopia, highlands

signatureBuildings: round stone tukul with thatched roof
rectangular stone house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Ethiopia's highlands span many regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The highlands are cool and densely farmed, with round stone tukuls thatched with grass in villages and rectangular stone or mud houses under corrugated metal in towns; Addis Ababa is the largest city. Teff, coffee and barley are the main crops, with maize, sorghum and enset; coffee is the leading export. Rain comes mainly from June to September, with a short March-May rainy season and a dry October-February; snow occurs only on the highest peaks and is not typical in the lowlands. Soil erosion, deforestation and population pressure are major concerns.

name: Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia
notes: Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia span several regions and states, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coasts are hot and arid, with flat-roofed coral stone and plastered houses in old ports and corrugated metal in fast-growing towns; the highlands around Asmara are cooler. Acacia, frankincense, date palms and mangrove are the main trees, while sorghum, maize and sesame are the visible crops and livestock dominates the dry plains. Rain is irregular, with the Gu rains from April to June and the Deyr from October to December in Somalia; snow does not occur in the lowlands. Drought, conflict and displacement make data uneven.

name: Sahel (Senegal to Chad)

signatureBuildings: round mud-brick house with thatched roof

notes: The Sahel stretches from Senegal to Chad, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is semi-arid acacia savanna with scattered millet and sorghum fields, mud-brick compounds and round thatched houses; towns along the Niger and Lake Chad have flat-roofed adobe buildings and corrugated metal. Acacia, baobab, shea and date palms are the main trees, and millet, sorghum and cotton the main crops, with groundnuts and gum arabic. The single rainy season runs from June to October and the long dry season from November to May; snow never occurs. Drought, desertification and insecurity are persistent pressures. Mali, Niger and Chad north of about 16°N belong to the Sahara region instead (split by latitude).

name: West Africa coast (Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo and Benin)

signatureBuildings: concrete block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo and Benin span many regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The Gulf of Guinea coast is humid and densely settled, with linear villages and fast-growing cities of concrete block under corrugated metal roofs; thatch survives on older and rural houses. Cocoa, maize and cassava are the main crops, with oil palm, yams, coffee and groundnuts; Abidjan, Accra, Lomé and Cotonou are the largest cities. The coast has two rainy seasons, April-June and September-October, and a drier November-March period; snow never occurs. Deforestation, coastal erosion and urban growth are major issues.

name: Nigeria

signatureBuildings: cement block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Nigeria spans 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The south is humid forest and delta country, the middle belt is savanna and the north is drier Sahelian grassland; Lagos, Abuja and Kano are the largest cities. Cement-block houses with corrugated metal roofs dominate towns, while mud-brick compounds and thatch survive in rural areas. Cassava, yam and maize are the main crops, with rice, sorghum, millet and cocoa. Rain falls from April to October in the south and June to September in the north; snow never occurs. Oil pollution, flooding and rapid urban growth are major pressures.

name: Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia

signatureBuildings: round thatched hut with mud walls
timber house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia share the humid Upper Guinea coast, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is one of West Africa's wettest regions, with mangrove creeks, rainforest, rice swamps and scattered farms; Conakry, Freetown and Monrovia are the largest cities. Rural houses are mostly round or rectangular with mud walls and steep thatched roofs, while corrugated metal spreads along roads and in towns. Rice, cassava and cocoa are the main crops, with coffee, rubber, oil palm and fruit. Rain falls from May to October and the dry season runs from November to April; snow never occurs. Deforestation, mining and weak infrastructure make data uneven.

name: Greece: mainland and Crete

signatureCrops.name: vegetables under plastic in the Ierapetra greenhouse belt

notes: Greece is covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed; the Cyclades (gr-cyclades) and other island groups use their own regions where they exist. The air signature: grey-green olive groves over most hillsides, dark cypress spires along village lanes, whitewashed and stone houses under red-brown tile (stone-slab roofs survive in Epirus, flat concrete roofs in modern sprawl). Crete adds bare white mountains, the olive grids of the Messara plain and the Ierapetra greenhouse belt; Thessaly is the mainland's flat cotton-and-grain plain. Winter is the green season and the landscape parches gold from June. Lowland snow is rare; only the Pindus, Olympus and the White Mountains whiten.

name: Western Balkans (Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro)
notes: All four countries are covered whole. Three worlds meet: Slovenia's forested alpine hills with scattered farms and kozolec hayracks; the Croatian and Montenegrin Adriatic, where pale limestone towns under red tile crowd the shore and the bare karst behind is stone-walled sheep country; and green mountain villages on Bosnian and Montenegrin slopes under spruce-beech forest. The Pannonian east (Slavonia) is flat maize-and-grain country. Inland snow lies in winter; the Adriatic coast stays green and essentially snow-free.

name: Central Balkans (Serbia, North Macedonia, Albania, Kosovo)
notes: XK is the widely used user-assigned code for Kosovo (no official ISO code). All four territories are covered whole. Flat Vojvodina is striped grain and sunflower country; the Sumadija hills carry plum orchards around every homestead. North Macedonia's Vardar valley is dry sunflower and maize country between bare mountains; Albania is a steep green coast with olive and citrus terraces and minarets; Kosovo is a mountain-walled basin of small fields. The hills go dry gold in July-August.

name: Romania and Moldova

signatureCrops.name: sunflower and wheat on the steppe plains
vineyards on the slopes (Dealurile Moldovei, Codru)

notes: Both countries are covered whole. The Carpathian arc is beech and conifer forest with chain villages climbing the valleys; around it Transylvania's Saxon villages with fortified churches, Moldavia's monastery compounds, and the Wallachian and Bessarabian steppe plains of sunflower and wheat with vineyard blocks on the slopes. Haystacks dot the Maramures and Codru meadows. Winter snow lies inland; the plains go dry gold by August.

name: Bulgaria
notes: Covered whole. The Stara Planina runs across the country as a dark forested spine; north of it the Danube plain is striped grain country, south of it the drier Thracian plain. Between them lie the Valley of the Roses and small wine districts. Villages are low houses of stone and render under red-brown tile; Rhodope villages climb terraced slopes. Lowland snow falls most winters; the lowlands go straw gold in July-August.

name: Ukraine

signatureCrops.name: wheat, maize and sunflower field belts

notes: Covered whole. Vast straight-bounded blocks of wheat, maize and sunflower stitched together by poplar windbreaks along roads and field edges, with the Dnipro and its reservoirs cutting the plain. Whole districts go gold when the sunflowers bloom in July. Villages are single-street strings of whitewashed cottages under slate, metal and red tile, with golden-domed churches; forest-steppe to the north, bare steppe to the south; the Carpathians in the west. Lowland snow lies most winters.

name: Belarus
notes: Covered whole. A flat forest-and-marsh plain: pine and birch forest over much of the land, bog patches in the Pripyat basin, and small damp field strips around villages of painted timber cottages under metal or slate roofs. Red-brick churches mark the towns; Minsk is grey panel-block sprawl. Snow lies in winter; birches turn gold in September-October.

name: Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania)
notes: All three republics are covered whole. A broad flat plain of big striped arable fields, rape-yellow in May-June, between large blocks of spruce, pine and birch, with brown raised bogs and manor houses in alleys of old trees. Farmsteads are wooden houses under red tile or grey metal, loosely scattered; the coast is low pine and dune. Birches go gold in September; snow lies in winter.

name: European Russia: west and centre
notes: Subdivisions are federal subjects of the European west and centre (from the ISO 3166-2:RU page). Not yet covered: the European north (Murmansk, Arkhangelsk, Komi, Nenets), the south (Krasnodar, Rostov, Volgograd, Astrakhan, Kalmykia, North Caucasus) and the Urals; they need their own regions. Dark birch-pine forest and bog in the north, giant rye, wheat and potato fields in the centre, strings of timber izbas along roads and rivers, onion-domed churches above them. Moscow, St Petersburg and the Volga cities bring vast grey panel-block districts. Snow typically lies November to March; birches go gold in September.

name: Cyprus and Malta
notes: Both island republics are covered whole. Malta is one of Europe's densest landscapes, limestone towns merging into one stone-grey sprawl of flat roofs; Cyprus keeps stone villages among olive and carob groves, the flat Mesaoria grain plain and pine forest on the Troodos. Flat-roofed limestone and concrete, with solar water tanks on the roofs. Green November-March, straw gold from May. Snow only on the Troodos summit.

name: Cameroon and the Central African Republic

signatureBuildings: cement block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Cameroon and the Central African Republic span many regions and prefectures, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Cameroon runs from humid Atlantic rainforest and volcanic Mount Cameroon through savanna to the Sahel edge, while the Central African Republic is mostly Sudano-Guinean savanna with an equatorial forest south; Douala and Yaounde are the largest cities and Bangui is the CAR capital. Cement block and plaster houses with corrugated or painted metal roofs dominate the cities, with thatch-roofed wattle houses in rural areas. Cocoa, plantains, cassava, maize and palm oil are the main crops, with coffee, cotton and millet in the drier north. Rain falls from March to October in the south and May to September in the north; snow never occurs. Insecurity in the CAR and deforestation make data uneven.

name: Congo basin (DR Congo, Republic of Congo, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea)

signatureBuildings: cement block house with metal roof

notes: The Congo basin spans four countries, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is the world's second-largest tropical forest, with dense lowland rainforest, swamp and peatland crossed by the Congo River and its tributaries; Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other on the river, Libreville and Malabo sit on the coast, and Lubumbashi and Mbuji-Mayi are mining cities. Palm-thatch houses with wattle walls remain the rural majority while cement block under corrugated or painted metal spreads in the cities. Cassava and plantains are the staples and grow year round, with maize, yams, rice, groundnuts, palm oil and rubber. Rain falls all year with only short drier spells; snow never occurs. Conflict, poor transport and mining make data sparse and uneven.

name: Uganda
notes: Uganda spans many districts, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is fertile lake-land on the equator, with Lake Victoria, volcanic hills, tea country and the headwaters of the Nile; Kampala is the largest city. Iron-sheet roofs on brick or plaster houses are the norm on hillsides and in towns, with round thatched huts remaining in rural areas. Coffee, bananas (matoke), tea, maize and cassava are the main crops, with cotton and sugar. Rain falls in two seasons, March to May and September to November, with drier spells from December to February and June to August; snow never occurs in the lowlands. Rapid population growth, wetland loss and deforestation are pressures.

name: Rwanda and Burundi

signatureBuildings: rectangular brick house with iron sheet roof

notes: Rwanda and Burundi span many provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. These are the densely farmed thousand-hills highlands south-west of Lake Victoria, with Kigali, Bujumbura and Gitega the largest cities. Rectangular fired-brick houses under corrugated iron sheets have replaced most traditional homes, though conical thatched huts survive in rural areas and precolonial domical homesteads are remembered. Coffee, tea and bananas are the leading crops, with beans, cassava and sorghum as staples. Rain falls from March to May and September to December, with dry spells from June to August and around January; snow never occurs outside the highest volcanic peaks. Deforestation and soil erosion are serious pressures.

name: Tanzania (incl. Zanzibar)

signatureBuildings: Swahili coral-stone house with flat roof
brick house with corrugated iron roof

notes: Tanzania spans many regions and includes semi-autonomous Zanzibar, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The mainland runs from the Swahili coast across miombo and acacia savanna to the Rift Valley and Kilimanjaro; Dar es Salaam is the largest city and Dodoma the capital, while Stone Town is Zanzibar's old coral-stone centre. Corrugated iron roofs dominate towns, concrete flats are spreading, and makuti palm thatch remains typical in villages; Swahili coral-stone houses with flat roofs mark the old ports. Maize, cassava, rice and beans are staples, with cashews, coffee, tea, sisal and cotton as exports and cloves from Zanzibar. Rains fall from November to May and the long dry season runs from June to October; snow lies only on Kilimanjaro's shrinking ice cap, never in the lowlands. Deforestation and rapid urban growth are pressures.

name: Kenya, coast strip (Mombasa and Lamu)

signatureBuildings: Swahili coral-stone townhouse with flat roof

notes: This region covers only Kenya's coastal strip, split from the existing inland Kenya region at about 100 km from the sea; the interior, including Nairobi and the highlands, is covered by that inland region. The strip is the historic Swahili coast around Mombasa, Lamu, Malindi and Kilifi, with coral-stone townhouses and carved doors in the old towns, corrugated iron roofs in the growing towns, and makuti palm thatch along the beaches. Coconut palms, baobabs, mangoes and casuarinas line the shore, with coconuts, cashews, maize and cassava the visible crops and the port of Mombasa plus tourism the economic drivers. Rains come in the long season from March to May and the short season from October to December; snow never occurs. Coastal erosion, mangrove loss and tourism pressure are concerns.

name: Angola

signatureBuildings: cement block house with corrugated metal roof
Portuguese colonial villa with terracotta tile roof

notes: Angola spans many provinces including the Cabinda exclave, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The north is humid forest and coffee country, the centre is the Bie plateau, and the south grades toward the Namib desert; Luanda is a vast coastal capital and Benguela, Huambo and Lubango the next cities. Cement block houses with corrugated or painted metal roofs dominate Luanda's sprawl and its musseques, Portuguese colonial villas keep terracotta tiles, and thatch remains common in rural areas. Cassava, bananas, maize and coffee are the main crops, with oil and diamonds driving the economy. Rains fall from October to April and the dry season from May to September; snow never occurs. Landmines, post-war recovery and oil dependence shape the data.

name: Zambia and Malawi

signatureBuildings: round thatched hut in a fenced compound
fired-brick house with iron sheet roof

notes: Zambia and Malawi span many provinces and districts, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. These are plateau countries of miombo woodland, acacia savanna and the Zambezi and Lake Malawi basins; Lusaka and the Copperbelt dominate Zambia while Lilongwe and Blantyre anchor Malawi. Round thatched huts in fenced compounds are still the rural majority, with fired-brick houses under corrugated or rusted iron sheets in towns; Malawi's hand-fired brick houses are a notable craft. Maize is the staple everywhere, with tobacco, tea and groundnuts as Malawi's exports and copper mining driving Zambia. Rains fall from November to April and the long dry season from May to October; snow never occurs. Drought and deforestation for tobacco curing and fuelwood are pressures.

name: Mozambique

signatureBuildings: cement block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Mozambique spans many provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is a long Indian Ocean coast of mangrove creeks, coral islands and coconut groves behind which lie miombo woodland and the Zambezi and Limpopo valleys; Maputo, Beira and Nampula are the largest cities. Cement block houses with corrugated or painted metal roofs line the cities, macuti palm-thatch roofs remain typical in older quarters and villages, and mangrove poles still frame coastal buildings. Cassava, maize, cashews and coconuts are the main crops, with cashew a signature export. Rains fall from November to April and tropical cyclones strike the coast in that season; snow never occurs. Cyclone damage, coastal flooding and insecurity in Cabo Delgado make data uneven.

name: Zimbabwe

signatureBuildings: brick house with corrugated iron roof
round thatched hut with mud walls

notes: Zimbabwe spans ten provinces, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is highveld plateau country between the Zambezi and Limpopo, with the Eastern Highlands on the Mozambique border and dry lowveld valleys; Harare and Bulawayo are the largest cities. Brick houses with corrugated iron roofs and plastered walls dominate towns and resettlement areas, round thatched huts with mud walls remain the rural norm, and clay tile roofs survive in older suburbs; the mortarless granite walls of Great Zimbabwe recall the region's medieval city. Maize, tobacco and cotton are the main crops, with cattle and gold. Rains fall from November to March and the cool dry winter from April to October brings highveld frost; snow falls only rarely on the Eastern Highlands peaks, not in the lowlands. Drought and economic instability shape the data.

name: European Russia: north

signatureCrops.name: golden reed beds in river deltas and lake shores

notes: Karelia (RU-KR) is listed with ru-west. Endless spruce-pine taiga over glacial bogs, brown peat rivers braiding to the Arctic, and almost no people. Tundra in the far north with reindeer herds and no trees; log villages with tent-roofed wooden chapels along rivers; blocky Soviet towns around Murmansk, Arkhangelsk and Syktyvkar and the smelting scars of the Kola Peninsula. Hay is the only real crop; lakes freeze in October and snow lies until May.

name: European Russia: south

signatureCrops.name: wheat, sunflower and maize on the black-earth steppe

notes: Crimea and Sevastopol excluded by design. Giant straight-sided fields of wheat and sunflower broken by poplar and locust shelterbelts, stanitsa villages as long single streets of whitewashed brick houses under red tile, grain elevators as the only skyline. The Kuban is rice and vineyard country; Astrakhan adds the reed-choked Volga delta and melon patches; Kalmykia is near-desert steppe with Buddhist khuruls around Elista. Winter is grey and mostly snowless; green April-June, gold from July.

name: North Caucasus republics

signatureCrops.name: maize and grain on the Stavropol plain

notes: The Stavropol plain is open grain country, but the signature view is the mountains: snowy Elbrus and the wall of the Greater Caucasus, pine and hornbeam forest on the foothills, stone villages stacked on slopes, in Dagestan and Chechnya watched over by medieval stone battle towers, with minarets beside Orthodox bell towers further west. Grozny and the resort towns are new glass and panel blocks. Lowland snow is brief; the high peaks hold it all year.

name: Urals
