signatureCrops.name: spring wheat east of the range

notes: Kurgan Oblast (RU-KGN) is not yet covered. A low, rounded, densely forested ridge, birch and pine with dark fir on the wetter west, larch and forest-steppe to the east, wrapped in a great industrial belt: mine headframes, steel works and haze around Yekaterinburg, Chelyabinsk and Magnitogorsk, dacha cabins in the birch woods. Bashkiria adds oil pumpjacks and sunflowers, Orenburg open steppe and salt lakes. Snow lies November to March.

name: Western Siberia

signatureBuildings: timber farmhouse in a forest clearing

notes: Kemerovo (RU-KEM) is not yet covered. The flattest giant on Earth: a bog-and-taiga sponge threaded by slow brown rivers, with oil pumpjacks and gas flares in Khanty-Mansi and Yamal and reindeer camps on the northern tundra. Villages run as single streets of timber houses along rivers; Omsk, Novosibirsk and Tyumen are grey block cities on the Trans-Siberian. The south turns to the Kulunda steppe of huge wheat fields and long ribbon pine forests, rising to the snowy Altai. Snow lies October to April.

name: Eastern Siberia

signatureCrops.name: oats and barley in small southern fields
alas meadows in the Yakutian permafrost plains

notes: Tuva (RU-TY) and Zabaykalsky (RU-ZAB) are not yet covered. Larch taiga on permafrost from the Yenisei to the Lena, hydro dams on the big rivers, and Baikal, a long slate-blue rift lake ringed by mountains. Yakutia is continent-sized tundra and taiga with scattered log villages, hay meadows in thaw-lake hollows, and Yakutsk's blocks on permafrost piles. Buddhist datsans around Ulan-Ude. The larch taiga turns gold in September; snow lies October to May.

name: Russian Far East

signatureCrops.name: hay and vegetable patches around villages
berry bogs and pine marsh (Sakhalin, north)

notes: Amur Oblast (RU-AMU) and the Jewish Autonomous Oblast (RU-YEV) are not yet covered. Wild coastlines and forests across seven time zones: Vladivostok's steep hills and bays with huge bridges, the Ussuri forest of Korean pine and Mongolian oak, Kamchatka's snow-capped volcano chain over stone-birch forest, foggy Sakhalin with oil piers, Magadan's gold fields giving way to treeless Chukotka tundra. Panel blocks huddle on the ports; lighthouses on the capes. Oak and larch turn in September; snow lies November into April.

name: Kazakhstan

signatureCrops.name: spring wheat in the northern belt
irrigated cotton and rice in the south

notes: Covered whole. The Kazakh Steppe: a near-treeless grass ocean, feather grass silver-gold by June, rolling into the bare Kazakh Uplands. Huge spring-wheat fields and grey farm towns in the north; irrigated cotton and rice oases with poplars along canals in the south; sheep flocks and yurt camps. Almaty sits in orchard country at the foot of the Tian Shan, wild apple groves above the city and Schrenk spruce up to the snow line; Astana is glass towers on the empty steppe. Real lowland snow mainly in the north.

name: Kyrgyzstan

signatureCrops.name: hay and potato plots around villages
cotton and maize near the Fergana edge

notes: Covered whole. A mountain country: the Tian Shan wall runs its length, snow peaks over deep blue lakes (Issyk-Kul with its Soviet sanatoria), dark spruce on the slopes, wide summer pastures (jailoo) dotted with yurt camps in July. Valleys carry chain villages with apricot trees and poplar avenues, hay and potato plots, and the wild walnut forests around Arslanbob. Valleys are hot and dry from July; poplars flash gold in October.

name: European microstates (Andorra, Monaco, San Marino, Vatican)

signatureCrops.name: hay terraces in the Pyrenean valleys

notes: Four tiny states in one entry; Liechtenstein is covered by the Switzerland and Austria region. Andorra: slate-and-schist villages and ski runs in steep Pyrenean valleys, Romanesque churches with short bell towers. San Marino: terracotta-roofed stone town on the wooded Titano ridge with its three towers. Monaco: a Riviera cliff of white high-rises over a marina. Vatican City is a walled precinct inside Rome: St Peter's dome and colonnade. Winter snow only in Andorra.

name: Russian interior: the six gaps
notes: The six federal subjects left over between the earlier Russian entries; codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:RU page and disjoint from ru-west. Kurgan is forest-steppe grain country; Kemerovo (Kuzbass) is coal country - open pits, spoil heaps and haze between taiga ridges; Tuva is a mountain-ringed steppe basin with felt yurt camps and larch taiga; Zabaykalsky is rolling taiga and steppe east of Baikal; Amur Oblast is big soy and grain fields along the Chinese border; the Jewish Autonomous Oblast is swampy taiga along the Trans-Siberian. Villages are single-street timber and render houses; cities are grey block towns at the mine gates. Snow lies October to April; the larch turns gold in September.

name: Brazil: Amazon (north)

signatureCrops.name: açaí palm groves on the floodplain

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:BR page (the North region's seven states); Mato Grosso's share of the rainforest and the rest of the Center-West fall outside these Brazil entries. The canopy runs to the horizon unbroken - an irregular dark-green billow stitched by huge meandering rivers, tea-brown with sediment or near-black where forest tannins rule, with oxbow lakes and flooded igapó along the banks. North of the great river the land lies across the equator, but the region is overwhelmingly southern-hemisphere. People hug the rivers: stilted thatch and timber houses, floating markets at Belém and Manaus, and Manaus's rubber-boom opera house glinting over the jungle. Along the new roads the forest ends in fishbone patterns of pasture and secondary scrub; in the dry August-October window, smoke haze dims everything.

name: Brazil: northeast

signatureCrops.name: sugar cane on the wet coastal strip

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:BR page (the nine states of the Northeast region). Three parallel worlds: a humid green coastal strip of sugar cane, coconut palms and mangrove channels with baroque colonial towns under red tile (Olinda, Salvador, Recife's bridges and Dutch-era forts); the cool agreste highlands of small farms; and inland the sertão - the caatinga, a thorny grey-green scrubland of cactus and twisted trees that only greens for a few weeks after the rains (February-May), then bakes pale gold. Cattle wander bare paddocks; flat-roofed brick houses cluster near drought reservoirs. Recife and Salvador are dense high-rise and pastel colonial mixtures.

name: Brazil: southeast and south

signatureCrops.name: coffee on the Minas and São Paulo hillsides

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:BR page (Southeast plus South regions); Goiás, the Distrito Federal, Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul are not covered by any Brazil entry. The Atlantic Forest survives as dark green islands in a landscape of coffee hills, sugarcane flatlands and eucalyptus blocks; Rio's bare granite cones rise straight from the sea, and São Paulo spreads as an endless grey-brown block city. In the south the plateaus turn to araucaria forest with distinctive umbrella crowns, waterfalls (Iguaçu) mark the Paraguayan border, and German- and Italian-settled valleys hold timber farmhouses, vineyards and grain. Everything drips in the southern summer (October-March); Minas browns briefly in the August-September dry. Winter frosts are routine, but lowland snow is rare - a highland curiosity.

name: Andes north (Colombia, Ecuador, Venezuela)

signatureBuildings: stilt house on the flooded llanos

notes: All three countries are covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed; the equator crosses Ecuador and southern Colombia, but the population and territory sit mostly north of it. Three vertical worlds: the Caribbean lowlands and Venezuelan llanos, an ocean of grass and scattered mauritia palms that floods in the May-October rains and pales dusty in the dry; the three Andean cordilleras, cool and green, packed with coffee slopes, eucalyptus, whitewashed colonial towns under red tile, and - highest of all - the páramo, where the silvery frailejone grows; and Amazonian forest toward the southeast. Ecuador's volcanic avenue lines snowy cones above the equator. Evergreen everywhere: no autumn, and permanent snow only on the glaciated peaks above roughly 4,800 m.

name: Bolivia

signatureCrops.name: irrigated asparagus, sugar and rice on the desert coast

notes: Bolivia is covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed; the Peruvian sierra is already done in an earlier region's data, so this entry stresses Peru's coast and Amazon slope, plus all of Bolivia. The Peruvian coast is hyper-arid grey desert cut by sudden green irrigated valleys, with Lima's ochre sprawl beneath permanent haze; inland the montaña slides into the same Amazonian forest. Bolivia stacks the vertical zones: the Altiplano at 3,800 m - tawny bunch-grass, potato and quinoa fields, adobe villages, the deep blue of Titicaca, La Paz spilling down its canyon rim - the green Yungas cloud-forest slopes below it, and the eastern lowlands of Santa Cruz's soy savanna and the Chaco's thorny quebracho scrub. The southern summer (December-March) is the wet green season; winters are dry and gold. Lowland snow does not fall - only the 6,000-metre cordillera holds it. (Peru stays with the pe-andes entry; this entry's Peru coast notes are kept for reference only.)

name: Chile
notes: Chile is covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. A 4,300-kilometre ribbon squeezed between the Andes wall and the Pacific: the Atacama in the north, the driest landscape on Earth - brown rock, salt flats, copper mine terraces and abandoned nitrate towns - then the Mediterranean center, where the matorral scrub greens briefly after winter rains, and neat valleys of vineyards, olives and orchards front snowy Andean slopes. South of that, rainforest lake country and Chiloé's shingled wooden churches, ending in Patagonian fjords and ice. The whole central valley reads as a garden at the desert's edge. Lowland snow is rare - it belongs to the Andes and the far south; the landscape is greenest in the August-October spring and parches golden in the December-March summer, with vines turning in April.

name: Argentina: Pampas and Buenos Aires
notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:AR page (Buenos Aires province and city, Entre Ríos, La Pampa, Santa Fe, Córdoba); the Litoral provinces (Chaco, Formosa, Misiones, Corrientes) are not covered by any Argentina entry. The flattest farming country on Earth: from 1,000 metres up there is nothing to see but an immense green-gold quilt of soy, maize, wheat and pasture, cut at right angles by roads and lines of eucalyptus windbreaks, with a lone estancia, windmill and cattle dip in each square. Towns appear as crisp grids of white houses, red-tiled or corrugated roofs and a church, with the grain silos and elevator towers of the railports. Buenos Aires spreads as a vast white-and-grey slab at the edge of the river. Winter (June-August) brings frost and a yellower land but almost never snow.

name: Argentina: Patagonia and the northwest

signatureBuildings: adobe church of the Calchaquí valleys

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:AR page; Cuyo (Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis) is grouped with the northwest, and the northeastern provinces are left to the notes of the pampas entry. Two empty wonders: the subtropical northwest, where rust-red canyons and cardón cactus desert rise into the green yungas cloud forest and Tucumán's sugar-and-citrus plain, with adobe villages and high vineyards at Cafayate; and Patagonia, a wind-scoured tan steppe of grey shrub and sheep stations, ending south in the beech forest and glacier lakes of the Andes, where the lengas set the slopes alight in April. Mendoza's desert vineyards sit directly under the snow wall of the highest Andes. The steppe is essentially always dry-gold; the brief green comes with southern summer rains, and Patagonian lowland snow falls mostly June-July.

name: Paraguay, Uruguay and the Guianas
notes: All five territories are covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed; French Guiana is a French overseas department (GF). Paraguay is the Chaco's flat thorny dry forest in the west and greener small-farm country in the east, with lapacho trees lighting up pink over the dry-season fields in August-September. Uruguay is the gentlest view in South America: an all-green roll of cattle paddocks, wire fences, kerosene-blue dam reservoirs and stone-clad hilltowns, no mountains, no wilderness, just grass. The three Guianas face the Atlantic: below-sea-level sugarcane and rice polders behind sea dykes (Guyana), Dutch wooden colonial cores as at Paramaribo, mangrove coasts, and behind it all the unbroken rainforest of the Guiana Highlands with its tabletop tepuis. The region is southern-hemisphere only because Paraguay and Uruguay pull it there - the Guianas themselves sit north of the equator and stay green while the south dries in July-September.

name: South Africa: Western Cape (Cape Town and the winelands)

signatureBuildings: whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouse with thatched gable
plastered town house with tiled roof

notes: Western Cape is one of South Africa's nine provinces. It has South Africa's only Mediterranean-type climate, with cool wet winters from May to October and warm dry summers from November to April, and fynbos shrubland on the Table Mountain sandstone hills. Cape Town is the legislative capital and the winelands towns of Stellenbosch, Paarl and Franschhoek sit among oak avenues. Whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouses with thatched gables survive on the wine estates, while tile and corrugated metal roofs cover the suburbs and townships. Grapes, wheat, apples and stone fruit are the visible crops, with citrus and olives in the warmer valleys; snow never falls in the lowlands.

name: South Africa: Highveld and interior (Johannesburg and the Free State)

signatureBuildings: brick house with corrugated iron roof

notes: The Highveld and interior cover several provinces. This is rolling grassland plateau at 1,300 to 2,000 m around Johannesburg, Pretoria and Bloemfontein, the gold fields of the Witwatersrand and the Free State maize and wheat belt. Brick houses with corrugated iron roofs dominate townships and country towns while concrete tile roofs cover leafy suburbs, with thatched rondavels surviving on farms and homesteads. Maize, sunflowers, wheat and cattle are the visible land use, with gold and coal mining scars nearby. Summer thunderstorms fall from November to March and dry, frosty winters run from April to September; brief snowfalls can dust the eastern Free State in cold snaps but are not typical across the lowlands. The Northern Cape's dry Karoo is grouped here.

name: South Africa: east coast and KwaZulu-Natal

signatureBuildings: concrete block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: KwaZulu-Natal is one of South Africa's provinces. The humid subtropical coast runs from Durban, Africa's busiest port, up the sugar and banana belt to Richards Bay, rising to the Drakensberg escarpment inland. Concrete block houses with corrugated metal roofs dominate towns and townships, painted metal roofs spread on new builds, and round thatched Zulu homesteads remain across the rural heartland. Sugarcane, bananas, maize, mangoes and macadamias are the visible crops, with beach tourism along the shore. Rain falls from October to March and winters are mild and drier; snow never falls at low level, only on the high Drakensberg peaks. Eastern Cape is grouped here with KwaZulu-Natal.

name: Namibia

signatureBuildings: German colonial villa with red tile roof

notes: Namibia spans many regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is the driest country south of the Sahara, with the Namib sand sea along the cold Atlantic coast, the Kalahari fringe in the east and savanna around Windhoek and the cattle ranches of the centre and north. Corrugated iron roofs and concrete block houses dominate towns and townships, while whitewashed German colonial villas with red tile roofs mark Swakopmund, Luderitz and Windhoek's older quarters; thatch stays on rural homesteads and lodges. Camelthorn, quiver trees, mopane and makalani palms are the signature trees, and mahangu millet, maize along the Caprivi and Orange River table grapes are the visible crops. Brief summer rain falls from December to March and the rest of the year is dry; snow never occurs.

name: Botswana

signatureBuildings: round thatched hut in a family compound
concrete block house with corrugated iron roof

notes: Botswana spans many districts, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. This is flat Kalahari sand country, with the Okavango Delta in the north, cattle posts and boreholes across the veld, Gaborone the capital and diamond mining the economic base. Concrete block houses with corrugated iron roofs are spreading through every village while round thatched huts in walled family compounds remain widespread in rural areas. Camelthorn, mopane, baobab and fever trees are the signature trees, and sorghum, maize and sunflowers are the small dryland crops, with cattle everywhere. Brief summer rain falls from November to March and the long dry winter from April to October; snow never occurs.

name: Lesotho and Eswatini

signatureBuildings: brick house with corrugated iron roof

notes: Lesotho and Eswatini span their own districts and regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Lesotho, the Mountain Kingdom, lies almost entirely above 1,400 m in the Maloti, and winter snow is typical across the high plateau from June to August, reaching the lowland towns most years; Eswatini runs from a cool highveld through the middleveld to hot bush lowveld, with big sugar estates near the Mozambique border. Corrugated iron roofs dominate, clay tile roofs survive on older town buildings, and stone-walled or mud rondavels with thatch remain the rural norm, very much so in Lesotho. Maize and wheat feed the highlands while sugarcane drives the Eswatini lowveld; summer rains fall from October to March and winters are dry and frosty.

name: Madagascar

signatureBuildings: highland fired-brick house with tile roof

notes: Madagascar spans many regions, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. The world's fourth-largest island runs from humid rainforest on the east coast, across the Laterite Plateau of rice terraces and Merina brick towns around Antananarivo, to dry baobab and spiny forest in the west and south. Thatched roofs with ravinala palm and wattle walls are the rural norm, corrugated metal spreads through the towns, and the famous red fired-brick highland houses with tiled roofs mark the Plateau. Rice is the staple with two harvests, and vanilla, cloves, lychees and cassava are the visible cash crops and food, with cyclones striking from November to April. Deforestation, biodiversity loss and fuelwood pressure are severe.

name: Mauritius, Reunion and Seychelles

signatureBuildings: Creole wooden house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Mauritius, Reunion and Seychelles span different islands and states, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used; Reunion is a French overseas department. These are tropical maritime islands with a warmer, cyclone-prone southern summer from December to April and a drier, cooler trade-wind season from May to November. Corrugated and painted metal roofs dominate, built for cyclones, while Creole wooden houses with jalousied verandas are the classic look and vacoa palm thatch survives on old and beach buildings. Sugarcane fields ring Mauritius and Reunion's coasts, tea grows on the highlands and vanilla, cinnamon, coconuts and fruit fill the Seychelles gardens, with tourism the leading industry everywhere. Snow never occurs; tropical cyclones and coastal development are the hazards.

name: Comoros and Mayotte

signatureBuildings: concrete house with corrugated metal roof

notes: The Comoros and Mayotte span different islands, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used; Mayotte is a French overseas department and the Comoros an independent union of three volcanic islands with Moroni as capital. Villages climb the volcano slopes in dense linear lanes of coral-rag and plaster houses, thatched roofs still the majority in the rural Comoros while corrugated and painted metal cover the concrete houses of Mayotte's Mamoudzou sprawl. Ylang-ylang plantations for perfume, vanilla vines, clove trees, coconut palms and rice paddies fill the valleys, on the world's leading ylang and vanilla islands. Rain falls from November to April with cyclone risk and the drier trade-wind season runs from May to October; snow never occurs.

name: Cabo Verde and Sao Tome and Principe

signatureBuildings: Portuguese colonial roca villa with tile roof

notes: Cabo Verde and Sao Tome and Principe span two separate island countries, so no ISO 3166-2 subdivision is used. Cabo Verde is dry volcanic Atlantic islands with Praia as capital, where the brief wet spell runs from August to October and drought and emigration have shaped a hardy, whitewashed building tradition; Sao Tome and Principe are equatorial Gulf of Guinea islands whose colonial rocas once made them the world's leading cocoa producer, with rain from October to May and a duller, cloudier gravana in June to July. Corrugated metal roofs dominate both, clay tile roofs survive on Portuguese-era villas and roca houses, and thatch lingers on worker houses and rural huts. Cocoa, coffee, bananas and coconuts fill the Sao Tome slopes while maize, beans and cassava cling to the Cabo Verde valleys; snow never occurs.

name: Solomon Islands and Vanuatu

signatureBuildings: palm-thatch village house on the shore
stilt house standing in lagoon water

notes: Groups the codes SB and VU, which share the same Melanesian look: volcanic high islands with deep jungle, reef-fringed coasts, big lagoons and turquoise shallows. Villages run in a single line along the palm shore, coral shallows grade from white sand to bright turquoise to deep navy offshore, and Honiara and Port Vila are the only cities. Palm-thatch houses on timber or woven-cane walls are still the rural majority, corrugated and bright painted metal roofs spread through the towns, and stilt houses stand over the lagoons of Malaita and the ni-Vanuatu bays. Coconuts and copra are the cash crop, with taro and cassava slash gardens on the hillsides. The wet cyclone season runs November to April.

name: New Caledonia and Wallis and Futuna
notes: Groups the codes NC and WF, both French territories with a strong European building layer. New Caledonia's Grande Terre is a big island with a reef-enclosed lagoon, nickel-mined red hills and the columnar araucaria pines of the Isle of Pines, while Wallis and Futuna are small crater islands with lagoons and thatched villages. Noumea shows hipped corrugated and red tile roofs on plastered villas, coral-stone churches stand in every village, and Wallisian houses still carry thatch pushed by typhoon-season rebuilding. Yams are the ceremonial crop, with cassava, coffee and copra. Wet season November to April with cyclones.

name: Micronesia (FSM, Palau, Marshall Islands, Nauru and Kiribati)

signatureBuildings: concrete block house with corrugated metal roof
stilt house over the lagoon shore

notes: Groups the codes FM, PW, MH, NR and KI, which look alike from the air: coral atolls and islets slung along reef rims around pale lagoons, plus Palau's green Rock Islands and Nauru's mined phosphate coral plateau. Villages string out in a thin line along the ocean side of the reef, concrete block houses with corrugated metal roofs dominate after decades of typhoon rebuilding, and older thatch and stilt houses remain near the water. Coconut palms, breadfruit and pandanus cover the narrow land, with swamp taro pits and copra drying racks. The Pacific blue deepens fast past the reef edge. The wet typhoon season runs July to November.

name: Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands

signatureBuildings: hotel towers along a reef-bounded beach

notes: Groups the codes GU and MP, the US Mariana Islands, which share one look: a volcanic island arc with hard reef flats, bright shallow lagoons at Tumon and Garapan, and US military airfields among the hotel strips. Villages sit in concrete grid streets of typhoon-rated block houses under hipped metal and concrete tile roofs; every roof is strapped down and plastic water tanks dot the yards. Flame trees redden the hills in May and June alongside coconut shores and ironwood town avenues. Small farms grow taro, breadfruit and melons for the island markets. The wet typhoon season runs July to December, and September storms are the big hazard.

name: Small Polynesia (Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Tuvalu, American Samoa and Pitcairn)

signatureBuildings: open-sided fale with a sheeted roof
concrete block house with corrugated iron roof

notes: Groups the codes CK, NU, TK, TV, AS and PN, the small scattered Polynesias: Rarotonga and Samoa's green volcanic domes ringed by reef and lagoon, Niue's raised coral cliff island, and the classic atolls of Tokelau, Tuvalu, the northern Cooks and Pitcairn's lonely triangle. Villages line the shore in single streets of open-sided fales now roofed in corrugated iron alongside concrete block houses, with church roofs standing out along the atoll strips. Coconut palms, breadfruit and pandanus dominate the band of land between lagoon and reef, with taro pits and small orchards. The cyclone season runs November to April and trade winds keep the rest dry.

name: Hong Kong and Macau

signatureBuildings: dense residential towers climbing green hillsides
fishing village of stilt houses at Tai O

notes: Groups the codes HK and MO, the two southern Chinese SARs, which read as one region from 3 km: walls of residential towers packed onto steep green islands and the Pearl estuary's reclaimed flats, with Macau's casino towers on the Cotai strip. Between the high-rise, three-quarters of the land stays green country park and banyan-shaded village streets, while Tai O's stilt houses and Macau's tiled colonial core hold the older character. Flat concrete tower roofs with water tanks dominate the roofscape, older village and temple roofs carry clay tiles, and traditional green painted tin roofs survive in the oldest blocks. Small market gardens and lychee orchards linger in the New Territories valleys. Wet typhoon summers run April to September with storms peaking July to September.

name: Brazil: Cerrado and the soy frontier

signatureBuildings: metal farm shed with grain silo

signatureCrops.name: soy and maize on the red latosol

notes: Covers Goiás, the Distrito Federal and Mato Grosso (codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:BR page); Mato Grosso do Sul is split off into the Pantanal entry. The Cerrado is a savanna of twisted, fire-sculpted scrub on deep red earth, and from the air the frontier reads as geometry: kilometre-wide soy blocks, cotton stripes, and hundreds of perfect green central-pivot circles that glow against the gold of the May-September dry season. In that dry season the ipê trees detonate into pink, yellow and white crowns with no leaves at all. Brasília is a modernist arrow of white concrete and glass between an artificial lake, unmistakable from above; Cuiabá and Goiânia are grey block sprawl. No snow, no autumn - just the wet green pulse of the southern summer.

name: Brazil: Pantanal (Mato Grosso do Sul)

signatureBuildings: line of wooden bridges on the Transpantaneira

signatureCrops.name: cattle pasture on seasonally flooded plains

notes: Covers Mato Grosso do Sul alone (code verified on the ISO 3166-2:BR page); the Pantanal's northern half lies in Mato Grosso under the Cerrado entry. The world's largest tropical wetland: from 1-3 km it is a giant green-and-tan sponge, floodwater spreading across the plains each southern summer (December-April) and shrinking back to grass, oxbow lagoons and duckboard-dry pools by August-October. Dark gallery forest threads every river; palm savanna and scrub cover the rest, with cattle fazendas on the levees and the Transpantaneira running south as a dotted line of 120 small wooden bridges. Campo Grande is grey concrete sprawl on the plateau edge. No snow, no true autumn.

name: Argentina: northeast (Litoral)

signatureBuildings: red laterite road junction in the forest

notes: The four Litoral provinces (Chaco, Formosa, Misiones, Corrientes; codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:AR page), completing Argentina. Misiones is a green wedge between Paraguay and Brazil on blazing red laterite soil: neat yerba mate rows under tall shade trees, araucaria on the crests, and the huge spray column of Iguazú visible for kilometres. Corrientes adds the Iberá wetlands - a vast marsh mirror studded with yatay palms - and rice paddies; Chaco and Formosa are thorn forest and palm savanna with cotton plots, some of Argentina's poorest and least dense settlement. Rivers are tea-brown and enormous; towns are small white grids under red tile. The southern summer (October-March) is wet and green; the interior pales gold briefly in August-September.

name: Falkland Islands
notes: A British Overseas Territory with no ISO 3166-2 subdivisions, so none are listed. signatureTrees is empty on purpose: the islands are treeless wind-scoured grass moor and black peat, with the famous whitegrass and boulder 'stone runs' striping the hills. Settlement clings to the coasts - a few hundred sheep stations with their wool sheds and bunkhouses, and Stanley, a little seaside capital of red, blue and cream corrugated-iron cottages with white trim. From the air the sea matters most: pale sand beaches with penguin and seal colonies, and dark kelp forests ringing the shores. The austral summer (December-March) is the green window; winter is grey, wet and windy, with only occasional brief snow flurries at sea level.

name: Gambia and Guinea-Bissau
notes: Both countries are covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. The Gambia is a slim country strung along its estuary: a brown-green tidal river lined with grey-green mangrove fringe, villages of round mud-brick and tin-roofed compounds along the banks, groundnut fields drying on every roadside, and a thread of tourist hotels at the Atlantic mouth. Guinea-Bissau adds the rice-and-palm deltas around Bissau, cashew groves nearly everywhere (the main export, harvested January-May), and the turquoise Bijagós archipelago offshore. Both sit in the northern tropics: the June-October rains turn everything lush green, then the dust-laden harmattan bakes the land pale gold from November to May. Towns are low concrete block and sheet metal; mosques and colonial-era houses are the landmarks.

name: Western Sahara
notes: A disputed non-self-governing territory under de facto Moroccan administration south of the berm, with no ISO 3166-2 subdivisions to list. From the air it is almost pure desert: pale hamada gravel plains, orange dune seas, and dry wadis, with the one strong colour note being the turquoise lagoon of Dakhla and its row of kitesurf camps and tomato greenhouses. Life clusters in the southern towns - Laayoune's flat-roofed sandy-render blocks, date-palm oases in the valleys, eucalyptus windbreaks - and in fishing piers along the Atlantic, where cold fog often cools the coast while the interior bakes. There is effectively no seasonal change: the whole territory stays tan all year, with no wet season and no autumn colour.

name: Greenland

signatureBuildings: colourful timber house with white window frames

signatureCrops.name: sheep pasture in the south fjords

notes: An autonomous Danish territory with no ISO 3166-2 subdivisions, so none are listed. signatureTrees is empty on purpose: the island is essentially treeless, with only small planted groves in the south. The inhabited strip is a lacework of ice-free coasts around fjords - every settlement a clutch of brightly painted red, blue, yellow and green timber houses with white window frames, standing against black rock and snow; the ice sheet behind them is a white plateau rising from the shore, and it covers over 80% of the island. Nuuk spreads as a small colourful hillside city of concrete and timber around its harbour. Sheep graze the south fjords in summer, glaciers calve into the sea, the tundra flares rust-red for a few weeks in September, and snow lies at the settlements from October to May.

name: Faroe Islands and Svalbard
notes: Two North Atlantic territories, both with no ISO 3166-2 subdivisions to list (SJ also covers Jan Mayen). The Faroes are 18 green islands with no trees: sheer grass cliffs dropping into grey sea, waterfalls, and villages of white-framed timber houses and churches under living turf roofs, stitched together by road tunnels and sheep tracks. Svalbard, 60% glacier and bare rock, is Arctic desert: dark mountains, glaciers, and reindeer on brown tundra, with Longyearbyen a tiny grid of colourful wooden cabins, coal-era remains and the seed vault beneath the airport. Neither has real trees (a single small planted grove in Tórshavn), snow lies from around October to May - all year on the glaciers - and the brief July-August green gives way to rust-brown tundra by September.

name: Crown dependencies and Gibraltar

signatureTrees.name: Scots pine and beech glen (Isle of Man)

notes: Four small territories, each covered whole with no ISO 3166-2 subdivisions to list (Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory; the Isle of Man, Jersey and Guernsey are Crown dependencies). Gibraltar is a dense wall of white-and-pastel apartments stacked against the west face of the Rock, backed by olive scrub, Barbary macaques and the airport runway crossing the isthmus. The Isle of Man is open moor and gorse hills with glens of pine and beech, whitewashed stone farmhouses and the lochs of the interior. Jersey and Guernsey are green ridges of dairy pasture, early potato rows harvested for the Jersey Royals from April, and long belts of white glasshouses that glow in spring - all wrapped in tamarisk-fringed bays, forts and drying harbour mud. Lowland snow is rare and brief; the islands stay green most of the year, with modest autumn colour in October-November.

name: Guatemala and Belize
notes: Two countries covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. Guatemala is a volcanic highland of conical volcanoes above a checkerboard of maize patches climbing impossibly steep slopes, pine-oak forest, and dense Maya villages of concrete block and corrugated metal with an occasional thatched kitchen; Antigua sits in its old colonial grid under three volcano cones. Belize drops to flat low jungle, savanna and the hemisphere's second-longest barrier reef, with coconut palms on the cayes, cane fields in the north and citrus in the centre; its coast takes hurricanes directly (June-November). The rainy season is June-October, and the dry February-April haze burns the highlands gold.

name: Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua

signatureBuildings: volcano cone over a colonial town
banana loading pier on the north coast

notes: Three countries covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. El Salvador is the densest view: tiny fields and coffee slopes patchworked to the horizon, packed against a line of Pacific volcano cones. Honduras adds the big banana and pineapple plantations and palm-oil blocks of the Sula plain, pine-covered ridges, and the near-empty Moskitia rainforest; Nicaragua brings the two great lakes with island volcanoes (Ometepe), cattle country in Chontales, and the green Atlantic coast. Rural housing is everywhere concrete block and corrugated metal; colonial grid towns and grey concrete city centres sit under the volcano line. Hurricane season is June-November (Eta and Iota devastated the north coast in 2020); rains fall June-October, then February-April browns the Pacific side.

name: Costa Rica and Panama

signatureBuildings: container ships queuing at the canal
coffee town on a green ridge

notes: Both countries are covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. Two green isthmus nations: Costa Rica's volcanic spine, cloud forests, banana rivers on the Caribbean side and coffee ridges; Panama's canal, a straight artificial line of white ships through rainforest, and the roadless Darién gap closing the map toward Colombia. Cattle pasture and pineapple blocks fill the Pacific lowlands; the coasts are coconut and mangrove with sport-fishing lodges. Rural houses are metal-roofed concrete block; San José and Panama City rise as real skylines of glass towers. These sit mostly south of the hurricane belt - storms are rare - and the Pacific side goes dry gold from December to April while the Caribbean slope stays green.

name: Cuba

signatureBuildings: Malecón seawall and old Havana grid

notes: Cuba is covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. A long flat limestone island of soft greens: huge cattle pastures dotted with tall feathery royal palms, canefields in blocks with their rusting central mills, and tobacco fields around Viñales under white shade tents and beside their long drying barns. Villages are grids of one-storey concrete and faded pastel render houses with galvanised roofs; Havana adds its walled colonial grid, Malecón seawall and grey apartment slabs. Flamboyán trees drop red blooms over everything in early summer. The hurricane season (June-November) strikes the island regularly; the dry season ends with a brief March-April golding of the grass.

name: Hispaniola (Dominican Republic and Haiti)
notes: Two countries sharing one island, both covered whole with no ISO 3166-2 codes to list. From the air the border is one of the starkest lines on Earth: the Dominican side is genuinely green - forested cordilleras with Caribbean pine, emerald rice paddies in the Cibao, cacao and coffee under shade, coconut palms on the east coast - while the Haitian side is largely bare tan-brown hills, cut by erosion gullies from charcoal cutting and crowded with tiny terraced maize plots and mango trees. Port-au-Prince and Santo Domingo both sprawl as dense concrete slabs with corrugated and concrete roofs. Hurricanes cross the island every season (June-November); the dry months are February-April.

name: Jamaica and Cayman Islands
notes: Two territories covered whole, so no ISO 3166-2 codes are listed. Jamaica from the air: the bumpy green spongework of the Cockpit Country karst, the Blue Mountains rising to over 2,200 m with coffee rows under cloud, cane fields and red open-pit bauxite scars - soil the colour of the dirt roads - along the centre, and coconut-lined white sand coasts with all-inclusive resorts. Kingston sits in its dry rain-shadow grid at the mountain foot. The Cayman Islands, 100 km north, are flat low coral islands: George Town's glass financial towers, pastel beachfront blocks, the famous Seven Mile Beach and diving reefs. Both lie in the hurricane belt (June-November); Jamaica is green May-November and browns on the south coast in the December-April dry.

name: Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands

signatureBuildings: Old San Juan walled grid and forts

notes: Three territories covered whole - a US commonwealth plus the US and British Virgin Islands - with no ISO 3166-2 codes to list. Puerto Rico is the biggest and greenest: the true rainforest of El Yunque, a limestone karst belt, dense pastures and plantain groves, and San Juan - a huge concrete metro with blue-cobblestoned Old San Juan and its forts at the core. The smaller Virgin Islands are drier and hillier: green-brown ridges dropping into white sand coves, giant yacht marinas full of masts, and low villas in the scrub. Spanish colonial grids rule the towns; roofs are tile, concrete slab and metal. Hurricane season is June-November - Maria and Irma wrecked these islands in 2017 - and the dry December-April turns the small islands golden.

name: Lesser Antilles north
notes: Nine territories grouped (Antigua, St Kitts and Nevis, Montserrat, Anguilla, Saint Martin, Sint Maarten, St Barthélemy, Guadeloupe, Dominica) - all whole islands with no ISO 3166-2 codes to list. They run the whole spectrum of the dry-to-wet Antilles arc: pale scrub-and-beach islands in the north (Anguilla, Antigua's 365 beaches, the Dutch-French casino strip of Sint Maarten, yacht-packed St Barts), mid-green volcano islands with old cane fields and fort ruins (St Kitts, Guadeloupe's Grande-Terre), and the black-green high rainforest of Dominica and Guadeloupe's Basse-Terre. Montserrat shows its eruption scars: the southern half under grey volcanic ash, the former capital a buried modern ruin. Towns are small concrete block and sheet-metal grids; hurricane season is June-November, and the driest months are February-April.

name: Lesser Antilles south

signatureBuildings: the Pitons rising sheer from the sea (St Lucia)

notes: Six territories grouped (Martinique, St Lucia, St Vincent, Grenada, Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago) - all whole islands with no ISO 3166-2 codes to list. Martinique and St Lucia are high volcanic cones in deep green with banana and cane below; St Lucia's twin Pitons plunge straight into the sea. Grenada is the spice island - nutmeg and cocoa groves over the whole green mass - while Barbados is the flattest and most touristed: a coral shelf of cane fields, white beaches, golf courses and Bridgetown's low sprawl. Trinidad is really South American: oil derricks, the black bubbling Pitch Lake, hills of rainforest and mangrove swamps full of scarlet ibis. Concrete block and metal roofs dominate; hurricane season is June-November with the driest months February-April.

name: Bahamas, Turks and Caicos and Bermuda

signatureBuildings: turquoise bank against deep blue water

signatureCrops.name: salt evaporation ponds (Turks and Caicos, Inagua)

notes: Three Atlantic territories, all whole with no ISO 3166-2 codes to list. The Bahamas and Turks and Caicos are barely-above-sea coral banks: from the air the water steals the show - impossible turquoise shallows over white sand against the deep blue of the Gulf Stream - with pine-barren islands, mangrove creeks, pink-sand beaches, flamingo-filled salt ponds and low pastel houses with tin roofs. Nassau is a dense pastel resort grid with cruise ships. Bermuda, far out in the open Atlantic, is a tiny green ribbon of golf courses, casuarina and cedar scrub, white stepped limestone roofs on pastel cottages and walled marinas. These islands sit squarely in the hurricane belt (June-November); the winter dry season is the mild tourist season.

name: Dutch Caribbean (Aruba, Curaçao, Bonaire)
notes: Three Dutch territories grouped: Aruba and Curaçao as constituent countries plus the Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba) - all whole with no ISO 3166-2 codes to list. These dry, sun-bleached islands sit outside the hurricane belt, and it shows: cactus-studded tan scrub, windswept divi-divi trees leaning constantly east, green parakeets in the kunuku fences, and long golden drought broken only briefly by the October-December rains. Willemstad is the postcard - a small harbour spanned by a pontoon bridge and lined with gabled Dutch colonial houses in pink, orange and blue under red tile. Bonaire adds its flamingo-stained pink salt pan rectangles and the bright teal of the dive coast; Saba is a single green volcanic cone with cottages below the rainforest top.

name: Canada: Atlantic (Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, PEI, Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon)

signatureBuildings: fishing shed and wharf at the shore
painted wooden house with pitched shingle roof

notes: Groups CA-NL, CA-NS, CA-NB and CA-PE into one Atlantic look, plus the French islands of Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon (code PM), which are filed with countries CA and PM because they ride the same cold sea. From 1-3 km this is forested granite, fjords, fog and outports: single streets of painted wooden houses and fishing sheds running down to wharves on cold grey-brown water. Balsam fir and black spruce cover the barrens, with birch and maples in sheltered valleys turning gold and copper in late September and October. Small farms grow potatoes and hay, and wild blueberry barrens show low blue-green patches in August. Lowland snow lies reliably from November to April.

name: Canada: Quebec and Ontario

signatureBuildings: Victorian brick rowhouse under a steep shingle roof
red barn with a metal roof beside a grid of fields

notes: Groups CA-QC and CA-ON, the two most populous provinces, where the Great Lakes-St Lawrence corridor reads as city, suburb and soybean field in turn. Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal pile brick rowhouses and condo towers under dark asphalt shingle roofs, cream vinyl siding and grey flat tar rooftops, and red metal barn roofs spread across the farmed lowlands. Northern parts of both provinces fall back into boreal spruce and lakes, which is what a plane mainly sees away from the metropoles. Sugar maples blaze red-orange across the hills in late September and October, the classic maple-syrup forests. Lowland snow covers the ground from December to March.

name: Canada: Prairies (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta)

signatureBuildings: farmyard of metal barns in a mile-square field grid

notes: Groups CA-MB, CA-SK and CA-AB as one prairie look: flat grain country drawn on a mile-square survey grid, visible from 3 km as rectangles of wheat, canola and stubble in gold and olive. Towns are strict grids of one-storey houses with grain elevators beside the rail line; farmyards hold grey and red metal barns, quonsets and grain bins. Trees appear only as aspen bluffs, poplar shelterbelts and spruce windbreaks, with aspens turning bright gold in September and October. Canola blocks paint soft yellow in June and July and combines cut everything gold in August. Lowland snow arrives in November and holds to March.

name: Canada: British Columbia

signatureBuildings: wooden house with a cedar shake roof on a mountainside
glass condo towers backed by snow peaks

notes: CA-BC is one region because the whole coast and interior share the same west-coast look: steep dark-green temperate rainforest of Douglas fir, red cedar and hemlock falling to fjords and the Georgia Strait. Vancouver and Victoria grow glass condo towers and low wooden houses, many with the region's classic brown cedar shake roofs; clear-cuts show pale slashes on the mountains. The Okanagan Valley is a dry pocket of apple orchards, vineyards and lake-blue water. Coastal lowland towns are rainy and almost snow-free in winter, but October colours the bigleaf maples and interior larches gold.

name: Canada: North (Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut)

signatureBuildings: hamlet of small houses propped above permafrost ground
fuel tank farm beside the airstrip

notes: Groups CA-YT, CA-NT and CA-NU as the Canadian North, drawn the same at this scale: white and brown tundra, grey glacial lakes and lichened shield with permafrost under everything. The signatureTrees and signatureCrops arrays are empty on purpose because most of the region lies at or above the treeline and there is no visible field agriculture; only stunted black and white spruce survive in southern valleys. Small hamlets string along the water as single streets of modular houses with metal roofs, snowmobiles and fuel drums beside gravel airstrips. Snow lies from September to May, leaving a brief green tundra bloom of moss and sedge in June to August.

name: Mexico: North and Baja California (desert and maquila cities)

signatureBuildings: metal-roofed maquila shed beside the border highway

notes: Groups eleven northern desert states (MX-BCN, MX-BCS, MX-SON, MX-CHH, MX-COA, MX-NLE, MX-TAM, MX-DUR, MX-SIN, MX-ZAC, MX-SLP) into one dry north. From the air this is tan and pale-brown desert broken by saguaro-studded bajadas, copper smelters, and the big border cities of Tijuana, Ciudad Juarez and Monterrey, where flat-roofed concrete block houses in bright painted colours climb the hills and industrial maquila sheds run along the highways. Pivot circles of cotton, wheat and winter vegetables glow green and pale gold in the desert creases, especially in Sinaloa and around Culiacan. Summer monsoon rain greens the east in July to September while Baja stays bone dry; lowland snow is a rare freak and is not drawn.

name: Mexico: Central highlands (Mexico City, colonial towns and volcanoes)

signatureBuildings: colonial grid town with red-tiled church towers
flat-roofed painted block house with a water tank

notes: Groups the central highland states MX-CMX, MX-MEX, MX-PUE, MX-TLA, MX-HID, MX-QUE, MX-GUA, MX-AGU, MX-JAL, MX-MIC, MX-MOR, MX-NAY and MX-COL, the Trans-Mexican volcanic belt. Mexico City's endless grey flat roofs and Puebla's red tile colonial centres sit under the volcanoes Popocatepetl, Iztaccihuatl and Pico de Orizaba. Every flat roof carries a bright plastic water tank; the hillside milpas are drawn as banded terraces of maize and beans, and Jalisco's blue agave fields read as geometric olive rows. Rains run June to October, winters are dry and dusty, and snow never falls at town level.

name: Mexico: South (Oaxaca, Chiapas, Guerrero, Veracruz, Tabasco)

signatureBuildings: painted block house with corrugated metal roof

notes: Groups the southern tropical states MX-OAX, MX-CHP, MX-GRO, MX-VER and MX-TAB: green mountains falling to humid Gulf and Pacific coasts, with the famous windy gap of Tehuantepec between them. Villages run along the roads as linear streets of painted block houses under corrugated metal, with open palapa thatch shelters by beaches and markets. Shade coffee climbs the Oaxaca and Chiapas slopes in stepped banks, sugarcane and banana fill the Veracruz and Tabasco lowlands, and giant ceibas stand over the towns. Rains run May to October with a dry, dusty winter; snow never occurs.

name: Mexico: Yucatan peninsula

signatureBuildings: beach resort towers behind white sand

notes: Groups MX-YUC, MX-CAM and MX-ROO as one flat limestone peninsula: low green karst jungle with no rivers, cenote sinkholes, and a turquoise-to-teal Caribbean gradient along the Riviera Maya. Cancun's resort towers stand on white sand behind palms while Merida and the village capitals stay flat-roofed cream and pastel concrete block with palapa thatch at the beach communes. Milpa maize patches, straight henequen rows and lime orchards cut the scrub. Rains run May to October with hurricane risk in August to October; snow never occurs.

name: Remote ocean islands (Atlantic, Indian Ocean and subantarctic)

signatureBuildings: white plastered terrace on a wharf
coconut palms over a lagoon jetty

notes: Groups ten singleton codes that carry no other region: SH (Saint Helena), IO (Diego Garcia), NF, CX and CC (the Australian tropical islands), TF, GS, BV and HM (the subantarctic islands) and UM (the US minor outlying atolls). The tropical group shares one look: tiny seaboard towns with white plaster and corrugated iron, coconut palms, casuarinas and Norfolk pines, lagoons at Cocos and Diego Garcia and red-crab jungle on Christmas Island. The subantarctic group (TF, GS, BV, HM) is treeless, wind-scoured tundra with winter snow shown in the June to August snowMonths. UM mostly means empty atolls and airstrips, so the region stays sparse throughout.

name: Antarctica

signatureBuildings: research station raised on steel legs
fuel tank farm and wind turbines beside the airstrip

notes: AQ is the whole continent with no planted agriculture or trees: the signatureTrees and signatureCrops arrays are empty on purpose. From the air it is ice sheet, blue ice runways, nunataks and the white shelf edge, with the research stations as the only built things, mostly flat and raised on stilts or gravel pads against the snow, in pale panels and metal. McMurdo, the largest station, adds tank farms, wind turbines and rows of cargo. Snow is drawn every month; the brief summer light brings liquid melt streams in December to February but nothing greens.

name: US Mid-Atlantic

signatureBuildings: Manhattan skyline and grey suburban cul-de-sacs

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page. The Boston-to-Washington megalopolis at its centre: from 1-3 km an endless carpet of grey-brown asphalt-shingle suburbs with cul-de-sacs, big-box roofs and parking lots, stitched by eight-lane highways, that finally frays into the long parallel forested ridges of the Appalachians and the horse farms of Pennsylvania. The Chesapeake Bay drowns the river mouths in a maze of coves with corn fields right to the waterline. Deciduous oak-maple forest everywhere, flaming russet in October; snow is normal from December to February, heavier upstate; summers are green and humid.

name: US Southeast

signatureBuildings: white cotton fields of the Mississippi Delta

signatureTrees.name: live oak and longleaf with palmetto

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page. An ocean of planted loblolly pine in straight rows over red clay, broken by flat cotton and soy fields with white bolls showing in October, cypress-gum swamps standing in black water, and the tight bluegrass horse paddocks of Kentucky behind white plank fences. The Gulf and Atlantic coasts are a ribbon of barrier islands, resort towers and marsh; Florida is flat palms, orange groves and Walt Disney World's swooping roads, with the Everglades' sawgrass sea at its southern end. Humid and green from March to July; snow falls only in the Tennessee-Kentucky-Carolina uplands, and hurricanes head for the coast from June to November.

name: US Midwest

signatureBuildings: red dairy barn with silver silo
grain elevator on the rail line

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page. The Corn Belt at its purest: a flawlessly rectangular chessboard of dark-tilled and bright-green corn and soy quarter-sections aligned to the township grid, with grain elevators marking every rail town, pivot circles sprinkled across the sandier soils, and red dairy barns with silver silos in Wisconsin's green hills. The Great Lakes edge the region with dunes and cherry orchards; Minnesota dissolves into ten thousand forest-ringed lakes; Iowa ends in bluffs over the Missouri. Heavy grey suburbs ring Chicago, Detroit and the Twin Cities. Winters are white from December to March, maples burn orange in October, and everything greens hard in May.

name: US Great Plains and Texas

signatureBuildings: grain elevator at every rail crossing

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page. The widest grid on Earth: mile-square wheat and corn rectangles running to every horizon on the High Plains, thousands of green pivot circles, wind farms on the ridges, and the dune-grass swell of the Sand Hills. Towns are every ten miles at a rail crossing - grain elevator, water tower, grey grain-train. Texas adds its own worlds: Hill Country live-oak slopes, huge cattle ranches on the southern plain, Houston's refinery flares on the humid coast, and the sprawl of Dallas-Austin. Trees only survive as cottonwood and pecan rows along the rivers. Winter snow is normal on the northern plains but rare in Texas; the summer gold lasts from July onward.

name: US Southwest and Mountain West

signatureBuildings: desert city grid with green pools

signatureCrops.name: irrigated hay pivots (Snake River, Colorado valleys)

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page. The red-rock West: layered mesas, slot canyons and Monument Valley buttes over sagebrush flats that run grey-gold to the horizon, with dark islands of pine climbing each mountain range and long lava flows gone green with brush. Everything human is irrigation: bright hay pivot circles in desert valleys, orchards along the rivers, and the vast glowing grids of Phoenix, Las Vegas and Albuquerque with a turquoise pool in every second yard. Salt flats and open-pit copper mines add their own geometry. Lowland snow falls on Colorado, Utah, Montana and Wyoming winters (desert cities get almost none); the July-September monsoon briefly greens the desert, which otherwise bakes from spring onward.

name: US Pacific coast

signatureBuildings: Central Valley orchard grid and canals
snow-capped volcano above the forest (Rainier, Shasta)

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page. Three stripes along the map edge: a dark curtain of redwood and Douglas-fir forest on the foggy coast, snow-capped volcanoes (Rainier, Shasta, Hood) standing over the Cascades, and then California's Central Valley - one enormous grid of almond, orange and vineyard rows laced with irrigation canals. The California hills are dry gold from June to September, vivid green only in the March-April spring; the Pacific Northwest is an evergreen sea with grey-weather Seattle and Portland at its heart, clearcut patches on the private timberlands, and circles of irrigation in the Columbia plateau. Los Angeles and the Bay Area spread as endless low stucco-and-tile sprawl. Lowland snow is rare in the valleys and normal only in the mountains; autumn colour comes late and bright in October.

name: Alaska
notes: One federal state covered whole (code verified on the ISO 3166-2:US page), so no other codes apply. Mostly empty from the air: a black-and-white spruce mosaic threaded by braided grey glacial rivers, muskeg flats, and tundra to the north with caribou trails and pingos; the Alaska Range and coastal glaciers close the horizon, and the southeast Panhandle is a fjord coast of dense rainforest and fishing towns. Settlement is Anchorage's grid and a scatter of villages, each with its gravel airstrip and no road out; Fairbanks and Juneau are small river-and-mountain towns. Farming barely exists outside the Matanuska valley's summer plots. Snow lies from October to April (longer in the interior), and the whole boreal landscape flares gold and rust for a few glorious weeks in September.

name: Green Spain (Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, Basque Country)

signatureBuildings: granite stone walls around tiny fields (Galicia)
eucalyptus windbreak around a cow meadow

notes: Codes verified on the ISO 3166-2:ES page (Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, Basque Country - the green Atlantic north, nothing like the hot Spain of earlier regions). From the air it is Britain's weather with Spain's colour: an intense small-field quilt of maize, hay and emerald cow meadow, walled with granite and slate, draped over wet green hills and drowned in eucalyptus and pine plantations. Cattle sheds sit in every hamlet; villages are stone-and-render houses under red tile and grey slate, strung along fog-draped rías with mussel rafts in Galicia's estuaries and port towns below the Cantabrian peaks. It rains in every month (wettest November-March), there is effectively no dry season, and lowland snow is rare and brief - just occasional winter dustings inland.

name: Canary Islands

signatureBuildings: volcanic caldera and black lava flows (Teide)

notes: Code verified on the ISO 3166-2:ES page (the whole autonomous community). A volcanic archipelago off West Africa: black and rust lava fields, the huge snow-dusted caldera of Teide in winter, and green laurel-forest gorges on the north coasts. From the air the signature is white - whitewashed villages spilling down ravines, tourist hotel belts on the south coasts of Tenerife and Gran Canaria - plus the pale rectangles of banana plantations under white shade mesh and Lanzarote's black-crater vineyards. Dragon trees, palms and cactus scrub fill the dry lowlands. Winter rain briefly greens the north (February-April); otherwise it is warm and dry year-round, with lowland snow never falling - only Teide's summit gets it.
